tleman described an experiment in drunkenness in which the victims were two monkeys. One of the animals treated to a libation of old whisky be- came drunk gradually. The other, dosed with new whisky, developed a spirit of drunken viohince within a few minutes. Some weeks later the ex- periments were repeated with an interchaage of whiskies between the two subj.cts. The result proved that it was the character of the whisky and not the constitution of the monkey to which the different kinds of intoxication were due. While there is nothing very novel in this, it was rather surprising to learn, on the authority of a medical witness, that the colliers of Kinross prefer whisky of the kind that makes a monkey violent.

- A fire broke out on Saturday in the stores at the Barrow Ironworks, and spread to the pattern and other shops. Damage to the extent of several thousand pounds was done, including the destruction of valuable pat- terns, before the four engines which had been summoned succeeded in getting the fire under. A fire which unfor- tunately resulted in loss of life took place in a tenement building near Fleet-street, Landon, on Saturday after- noon. The oatbreak occurred in a room occupied by a billsticker, his wife, and three children. Two of the little ones were left asleep, and a neighbour soon after- wards discovered that the room was on fire. When the mother arrived she made several brave attempts to get into the apartment, but she was driven back by smoke. A fireman afterwards affected an entrance, but he could not get as far as the children's bed, and when the fire was extinguishrd the children were found dead from suffocation. A poll was taken ,n Saturday of ;the ratepayers of Barntoz to denide whether the Free Libraries Act should be adopted. Sir J. T. Brunner. M.P., had offered to give a collection of books to form the nucleus of a library, and suggested that the school which he has recently pre- sented to the township should be utilised for library purposes. A parish meeting agreed by an overwhelming majority to adopt the act, but a poll was demanded. Out of 820 electors, only 227 voted, and there was a majority against the Act of 35.

folded arms and bent head. He felt that circum- stances were weaving a net through which it was impossible to break. To face unmoved the dying man's dim eyes turned entreatingly towards him was impossible. He glanced away. His mind was convulsed by conflicting thoughts. His common sense prompted him to say "No " to the demand that he should fulfil his engagement. Yet the tender, sympathetic side of his nature revolted at the idea of darkening, with a keen disappointment, the last moments of a fellow-creature's existence. Meanwhile there was silence in the room—a silence that quickly oppressed Dennis with a sense of fear. He looked anxiously at the sick man, who lay back deadly pale. It was a marble-like pallor —the pallor of death! i Hurriedly Dennis opened the door into the ad- joining room. t "Grace!" he cried, "come quickly! Your father is—" I There was no need to finish that sentence. One glance at her father told her that the excitement of the last few minutes had been too great for him. "Oh! Father—father! " she cried in agony, clasping his cold, limp hands. "4 Her cry of pain pierced his poor numbed :brain. He opened his eyes, glanced at her, then at ! Dennis. " Promise—prortise ? "he murmured beseechingly to the latter. i His voice, and the accompanying look, would :have melted a heart of stone. Dennis's hesitation I ;gave way completely before it. Thrusting from this mind all thought of the bitterness of the 1 .-onsequences, he answered firmly: "I promise." • 1 The look of intense gratitude that illumined the •dying man's face brought to Dennis a pleasant sense of having acted rightly. That look was succeeded by a strange stillness— ' ithe stillness of death. Dennis put his hand gently on Grace's shoulder and murmured: 1 "He is gone. I will take care of you, 1

- The suspicion that a turnover of Liberal Union- ists to the Liberal fold is going steadily on is grow- ing on both sides of politics. This is not based merely on the results of by-elections, though they Count for a great deal. There are other signs, of which the Unionist agents,especially,it is said,in the Midlands and the North of Englanilare fully aware that the Unionist Nonconformists at all events are showing a growing lukewarmness in their attach- ment to the Ministerial cause. Of course there is a disposition to put this down mainly to the atti- tude of the Government upon educational ques- tions ; and to this, no doubt, was attributable the beginning of any movement towards the Liberal party. But I find among experts at the present time a disposition to regard the recent develop- ment of our foreign and colonial policy, and espe- cially Mr. Chamberlain's share in them, as having been at least equally effective in the matter. The indiscreet letter written by Senor Don Enri- que Dupuy de Lome, the late Spanish Minister to the United States, whi.,. to his recall, was not the first occasion of uncompliniei.:-,- •ferences he bad made to thst country. Rather mu i than twenty years ago he published a book entitled "From Mad- rid to Madrid around the World," which contained expressions of opinion that were brought up against bim when he was appointed to Washington in 1892. He described the American woman as "adventurous and bold,spendthritt,elegant,and wearing the most risky fashions, protected more by the fear of the law than by the respect she inspires," while the Amierican man he said, among other unkind things, "a great patriot, he almost invariably robs his Country whenever he is called to its service."

Among the many wrongs suffered by Ireland was the enforcement in pest times of statutes compell- ing many Irishmen to relinquish the use of the pre- fix "Mac" or "0" before their names, these prefixes being indicative of Royal or lofty lineage. This Mr. Macaleese seeks as far as possible to remedy by means of the bill which he brought in on Tuesday. Me is supported by Mr. Daly, Mr. W. Jones, Mr. W. Redmond, Mr. E. M'ilugh, and Mr. Patrick O'Brien.

I understand that the Local Government Board has given orders that the new vaccine mixed with glycerine is to he served out to all vaccination offi- cers at once. Some delay has arisen in sending out the new lymph, owing to the want of a special laboratory for the cultivation of the matter.

An early opportunity is to be taken by some of the military critics of the Government in the /louse of Commons to draw attention to the adoption of quick-firing guns for the field artillery of Germany and France. The former country has now five or six army corps supplied with new or converted quick-firers, and France is following suit as fast as the guns can be turned out. She has now three army corps equipped with them. Nothing has ap- parently been done in this direction by our War Office, although they admit knowledge of the ac- tion of Germany and France. Indeed, it is proposed during the coming year to increase our field artillery by nearly 100 pieces, but all of the current pattern, which is not quick-firing. It is held that the orders now in hand for what are in effect obsolete;field pieces should be cancelled.

Lord Salisbury's illness has attracted a natural amount of attention in the lobby. There have been rumours for many months that his lord- Ship's health has no been good, but that has never interfered with the discharge of his official duties. The fact, probsbly is that his vitality and energy nave been greatly lowered by the immense strain of his Foreign Office work. His post there has been more of a hurdt,n then if the country had been in- volved in act ual war. From day to day he has scarcely kr.nv.n what it was to eee the country otherwi L !lid verge of a precipice, and therefore he dres not meet eves a slight attack of influenza with a Puperabundance of strength to bear it.

The military autlicrities bare yielded with per- fectly good grac- to Mr. Patrick O'Brien 's sugges- tion that such Irish soldiers as desire it might be allowed to wear the shamrock on St. Patrick's Day. That a number of enthusiastic Irishmen will do so is beyond all doubt, and it is just as certain that some hot-headed or murtinet colonels will COMO In- to unnecessary collision with them on the Alabject. The matter is one of perfectly harmless sentiment, and if freely sauc'ioned, or it left unnoticed by the superior officers, might soon become a matter of in- difference among the men. Intolerance begets re- sistance, and definitely Inc-ns the bon i between officers and men. L,,Nldt:F. a possibility should be removed of anyone making political capital out of such a trifle.

The greal unicro and i7isccintions which repro-1 sent labour are early in the field this year with their arrangements for the annual lilav day demon- stration. It will bo held in Hyde Park as usual, and there is every prospect of the gathering being very much larger than hitherto. The delegates, to the number of nearly a hundred,representing Social- ist and non-Sociali:-:, orc;.ietions. are united and eno,usiastio, and it i expect' that the recent en- Rineers struggle will Lave produced such a marked solidarity of feeling among the workmen as to break down the antipathy of the older unions to the new ideas which form the creed of the more advanced :vchhoooalr.e eTrh geanfit,oriwnward section of the labour leaders " eff ct of the strike anxiety to the the demonstration are looking fo-ward with curiosity rather than upon the more cowervative In ions, but they must not bo too sanguin 3 in their expectations about a large accession to their numbers just yet.

div.head: (Copyright.)
div.p: (Copyright.)
THE WHEEL OF FATE.
BY MRS. BAGOT HARTE. Author of "Love's Revenge," "Bianca," "The Silver Lining," &c., &c.
CHAPTER XI.

The Tewsers lived in a dingy back street leading from the Marylebone-road. It was one of those streets where the houses are sub-divided amongst various families, and a general haziness exists as to whose duty it is to open the door. The knocker had been wrenched off many years before, and the bell only emitted a feeble tinkle. But as no one ever paid formal calls at No. 3, South Street, these defects were not thought worthy of consideration by the inmates.

Dennis rang twice, but no one came in response. The basement tenant came out into the area and surveyed him; then, mentally deciding that he was not in quest of her, retreated indoors again and shut the door with a bang. He glanced up at the first-floor windows, suspecting they belonged to the Tewsers' rooms. A dirty lace curtain was being wafted about by the breeze, and the windows stood open, clearly indicating that the tenants were superior to the average South Street tenants, who appeared to be unanimous in considering fresh air as a thing to be carefully excluded from rooms. After knocking a7ain and waiting a few minutes longer on the doorstep, he came to the conclusion that the best thing to do, under the circumstances, was to enter the house and inquire from any inmate he might chance to see, which rooms the Tewsers occupied. Acting upon this decision, he opened the door quietly and walked in. As he stood waiting in the hall, he suddenly became aware that inquisi- tive eyes were watching him from behind a half- open door. Apparently the owner of those eyes was more than satisfied with hit appearance, for she put her head into the hall and said in a most friendly 'voice: "What do you want? Ma's out." "Will you kindly tell me which are Captain Tewser's rooms? " inquired Dennis. "Him as is dying? " asked the child with great interest.

"I did not know he was ill." "Yes; he's uncommon bad. He'll never get no better, ma says. She's going to offer to wash their lace curtains for the funeral day. I've never been in a 'ouse where there's been a funeral from yet, and "—with growing animation—" Ted and ine's going to stay at home to—" "Kindly tell me which are Captain Tewser's rooms," interrupted Dennis. "They've got three rooms on the first floor."

Dennis went slowly upstairs and knocked gently at the first door he came to. It was instantly opened by Grace. The moment that she saw who had come the colour rose to her cheeks, and a joyous gleam shot from her eyes. Then, as she realised that he was regarding her with an expres- sion which lacked the faintest suggestion of affection, she became deadly pale. "I am sorry to hear that your father is very ill," he said, with an effort to appear sympathetic, after the usual salutations had been exchanged. "Yes, very ill," she answered quietly. "Will you come at once and see him? He has been asking for you often, lately." "But is he well enough to see me? The excite- ment might be very injurious for him. Would it not be best to consult the doctor first? "Father has already done so, and "—here her voice was low and husky—"the doctor said that any excitement might hasten the end by a few hours, but that nothing could make any positive difference." "I am very sorry for you." This time Dennis spoke with genuine feeling. For a few moments there was silence. Dennis leaned with his elbow on the chimney-piece, glancing critically at the tall, fair, careworn girl before him, who held herself with superb grace and dignity, notwithstanding the trying circum- stances in which she was placed, and the sordid poverty by which she was surrounded. Another fact also surprised him. She shewed no disposition to treat him otherwise than as an ordinary friend. He had had a glimmering idea that she would be effusively glad to see him, but her manner was absolutely cool and collected, and lacked the faintest suggestion of affection. He was relieved at this discovery; yet, man-like, he was somewhat piqued. "Come and speak to my father, please," said Grace, opening a door leading into the front room. "Here is Mr. Vane, father," she added in a sub- dtied voice. On a small bed screened entirely from the light lay Captain Tewser. His eyes, which still burnt with the vitality and energy of former days, formed a striking contrast to his leaden complexion and emaciated features. The terrible change that the approach of death had wrought in this formerly handsome and attractive man, struck Dennis with painful force. Ha grasped the outstretched hand gently and kindly, deep commiseration at heart. In the full enjoyment of health and youth himself, he felt acutely sorry for this older man, whose momenta on earth were numbered, and who had apparently undergone great suffering. "I am very glad to see you, Vane," murmured Captain Tewser. "I have come as quickly as I could," answered Dennis.

"Y"—Yes. I am sure you have." Then he added quickly; "I am dying, Vane—dying." "I am very grieved to hear it." "The thought that troubles me most is the thought of leaving Grace. It is sad for her to be all alone."

"Ethel is married, I hear," was the evasive reply. Yes; married well—very well." The Captain said this with a tinge of pride. Then his eyes wandered to Grace, who was standing motionless, with her face averted. "I want to have a few minutes alone with Vane," he added, speaking to her.
She turned hastily towards him, as the blood came surging into her cheeks. "Father, could you not defer it?" she began, in a hesitating, half-frightened Toice. "Is it wise to—"

"Go, child!" he exclaimed imperiously. "Is it kind to make rue waste my small remaining strength? Do you wish to hasten my end ? " "Oh, no father!" She threw herself on her knees at his side. "Forgive me." Vane moved away to the window and stood look- ing out on the dingy house opposite. Three children were waiting on the doorstep ; they pointed rt him and laughed. He turned quickly on one si,!e, hoping to escape their scrutiny. At that moment Grace leaned over her father and kissed him ; then left the room. Once alone with Dennis, there was a marked change in the dying man's manner. The excitement under which he instantly began to labour was dis- tressing to witness. For days he had been planning in his own mind how to open this conversation with reference to his daughter's engagement. Now that the critical moment had arrived, he found it impossible to collect his thoughts ; and this mad,' him distressingly anxious to pursue the conversation without a moment's loss of time. "Vane, I'm growing confused • my thoughts seem to be getting beyond my control It is difficult to tell you what I wanted. I must--" He ceased speaking. Then, after a moment's pause, he added in a weaker and feverishly pleading voice: "You will assist me—help me ? " "Yes, all in my power, answered Dennis sooth- ingly. "It is this. Grace is still engaged to you, and in the eyes of the world you are legally and morally bound to marry her. In a short time she will be homeless and an orphan. Promise me you. will act honourably, and that you will marry her? " "It is difficult to answer that question—quite— er--" Dennis stammered. "'But you may implicitly rely on my doing all can to repair-- 'Stop, for God's sake! " gasped the other. "That is too cruel—to talk like that! You loved her until you discovered my shortcomings. ',Tow I am paying the penalty for all—all—by a miserable death in poverty and suffering! Forget my—my shortcomings. Do not visit them on my child. Is it manly to do so? You have won her heart. She loves you still. You are bound in honour to marry her. Promise."

"I—do---not--" Dennis began with hesitation, then stopped. He was going to say "see ray way clear to make that promise," but a glance at the dying man's agonised face rendered him incapable of .finishing that sentence., . .

"You hesitate! Surely you—a man of hononr— will not clit.eso this moment to—to—bre:lli off tho engagement! Captain TmFer cenaed Fp-id:int; and gasped for breath. Every second his voice Was growing more painfully strained. "You—you cannot I" he continued. "A man who selects the moment when his Samote's father is dying to break

div.head: CHAPTER XII.
div.p: CHAPTER XII.

It was the evening of Captain Tewser's funeral day, and South Street had only just subsided into ;its normal condition of quietude. All day the excitement had been great, for the grandeur of the rfuneral arrangements had attracted much atten- tion from the inmates of the various houses. The fact that Dennis Vane had been the only mourner had also evoked considerable comment. IGrace Tewser was sitting listlessly in the front room—whence, but a few hours before, her father had been carried to his last resting-place. It was now transformed into an ordinary sitting-room, barely furnished, but scrupulously clean, the icleanliness being due to the energetic voluntary Ihelp of Mrs. Brown, the ground-floor tenant. The lace curtains had been washed and darned, and the carpet patched with a total disregard to the direc- tion of the pattern. The medicine bottles that had recently reigned supreme as chimney-piece orna- ments were replaced by two china shepherdesses and a blue glass monkey, lent expressly far the occasion by Mrs. Brown. The curtains had been tied hack with well-worn crape, so as to give a "mourning-like look to the room," to use her own words. Grace noticed with surprise the keen interest, almost pleasure, with which this friend in need had entered into the preparations for the funeral. But she found it necessary to treat her with studied distance, as she was evidently burning to know where and how Grace intended to live, and what relationship, if any, existed between her and Dennis.

"What a nice gentleman he is, to be sure! " she had observed on more than one occasion, speaking in a manner that inferred it was a leading remark. But she had never been able to elicit more than a murmured "Yes" from Grace in reply. But Mrs. Erown had inherited a romantic. nature from her mother, a circus-rider, which even the possession of a "trying husband " and three sickly children had failed to suppress. She therefore employed her spare time in weaving very pleasant prospects for the "parlour tenant," as Grace was generally called by the other inmates of the house. As for Grace herself, the days following her father's death were passed aimlessly and wearily. From the continuous activity, which night and day nursing entails, she had suddenly found herself with little or no occupation. This severe reaction from great responsibility to enforced idleness had been a severe strain on her self-control. When Dennis had said: "I promise," as Captain Tewser breathed his last, she had been too much engrossed with the agony of the moment to heed or even hear those words; and she had only a glimmering recollection of Dennis saying: "I will take care of you." Therefore, so far as he was concerned, her future was a blank. Quietly, as if performing nothing more than his duty, he had made all necessary arrangements for the funeral, and had shewn a determination to remain at hand and relieve her from all responsi- bility and expense. Whenever the recollection of their past engagement flashed across her mind, she thrust it aside as a subject which must be buried and forgotten. Now, that the funeral was over, she felt she was launched into the world, alone and penniless, and must at once endeavour to support herself. But vague indeed were her ideas on ibe subject of gaining employment. As she leant back pensively in the well-worn armchair, she looked strangely superior to her surroundings. Her new black dress set off her tall, graceful figure to advantage; and the very sombreness of her attire accentuated her attrac- tions, forming a strong contrast to her fair com- plexion and wealth of golden hair. Dennis had told her that he would call early in the evening, and lier thoughts kept drifting in his direction. Was he coming to say good-bye? She shrank from contemplating such a possibility. low lonely she would be after he had gone! Perhaps he was coming to speak to her about their engagement and that promise of marriage which had been a mere empty form, so far as he was concerned. If he mentioned the subject, she was fully prepared to give hint buck his freedom, unreservedly. But she hoped lie would let her retain him as a friend— her only friend! It was hard to be alone in the world—to Itave no one from whom she could ask advice. If only Dennis would let her consult him, it would render her life much happier. She was curiously unsophisticated, this girl, who had been reared amongst sharp, unscrupulous characters. As rarely happens, her disposition had passed unscathed, though exposed to influences that would have ruined a snore impressionable nature. She rested her face on her hands, and wonderingly thought of what he would sal, when she asked him to be always her friend. or an instant the careworn, troubled look faded from her face, only to return a moment later many degrees intensified. She raised her head from her hands, sighed, and glanced around, as if anxious to find some employment that might distract her thoughts; But everything was scrupulously tidy and neat. There was nothing for her to do. She shuddered. Was her life henceforward to be always useless and aimless ? At that moment she heard Dennis's voice on the stairs. Mrs. Brown was talking to him in an officiously friendly manner. In her estimation the loan of the shepherdesses and blue glass monkey had raised her to the level of an equal with the parlour tenant's friend. "Miss Tewser is a bit cast down, as is only natural," Grace heard her remarking. "But, as I was at-saying to Mr. Brown just now, she'll pick up nicely and soon look 'earty if she can get away for a change to, the sea. Margate's the place for her! I'm certain of that; and if you'd like to make arrangements with me to take her along of us, when we go next week--well, at least, there's no 'arm in my speaking of it—now, is there?" "None—certainly not," answered Dennis. Grace turned crimson when she overheard this conversation. With relief she noticed there was not a vestige of annoyance reflected in Dennis's face, when he entered the room a moment later.
"I have not called at an inconvenient time, I trust ? " he said.

"Oh, no: I am very glad to see you," responded Grace. "I was expecting you. I want to thank you so much for all you have done; you have been so very-7-very kind.' "You must-nut thank me," be answered point- edly. "I am glad it has been in my power to be of use to you." Grace raised her eyes gratefully to him. lie read in that glance that her father's words were true, and that she loved him- deeply.- lie knew that his path of duty led in but one direction. Ile was in honour bound to seize the urescnt opportunity to ratify their engagement and make definite arrangements for their wedding. He .Was surprised to find himself contemplating the immediate future with a degree of satisfaction that was totally unexpected. Ile knew he did not love Grace deeply; in fact, he shrank from analysing' the condition of his affections. Yet it was impos- sible to find any manner of fault with her, She was beautiful, with a beauty that fascinated him.

• ana which was rencerea many clegrees more charm- ing by her being wholly unconscious of it. Her manner was pleasingly dignified, yet sympathetic, and her whole bearing that of a well-born woman. That she was friendless and penniless was her calamity, not her fault, and one that marriage with him Would effectually remedy. He drew his chair nearer hers and began toying with his watch-chain, as was his habit when thinking deeply. Then, realising that the subject must be opened at once, he turned towards her and placed his hand on hers. "Grace, we have been engaged many years now," he said.

"Yes," she concurred, with rising colour. "The time has come when our marriage should take place. Don't you hinir so?" She started, and looked at him with surprise and joy. She could scarcely realise that the man she adored, had adored for years, had remained faithful to her and was now suggesting she should become his wife. It was an intensely happy moment. "Yes," she answered simply. "If you really wish it.
"It is as you wish too, Grace," lie answered, with a shade of disappointment. "Do you still care for me I—love me!" _
"Yes-0 Dennis, I love you dearly. Can you doubt it ? " . .

"No; I do not doubt it." He spoke in the same quiet, undemonstrative voice as before; then leaned down and kissed her, adding: "You are quite satisfied, Grace, and are willing that the wedding should take place as soon as possible? " "Yes." Her manner of saying it was com- pletely free from hesitation. Dennis gave a sigh of relief. But it seemed to him a curiously brief way of ratifying a previously- ignored vow. He wondered if she knew that pressure had been used to win him back to keep- ing his promise. He hoped not; and fervently trusted that she never would. He was annoyed to find himself taking a prosaic view of their marriage, and wondering if they would be happy or not. Suddenly Grace's face became grave—strangely grave for one, that, but a short time before, had reflected so much joy and happiness. Dennis noticed it with faint misgivings. "God grant that we may be happy together!" be said fervently. "Yes—oh, yes! " she answered, striving to speak calmly. "You are so kind and--" Her trembling lips could say no more. Hastily she withdrew her hands from his and pressed them against her face. "Poor Grace !" he said gently. "You have had a hard life lately. I shall take you abroad at once. You want change and rest."

div.head: CIIA_PTER XIII.
div.p: CIIA_PTER XIII.

"Dennis. how I wish that to-day could last for ever! " exclaimed Grace Vane, as she and her husband were driving through the beautiful woods near Baden-Baden. "That's a most unattainable wish, Grace. W:iy do you wish it 7 " "Because I am so intensely happy." "But to-morrow you will not be a whit less happy, I hope," said he, as he carefully cut off the end of a cigar and lighted it, in a leisurely, absent-minded manner. He somewhat resented the tone of his wife's last remark. It was not often that she allowed herself to express her feelings thus frankly ; and on this occasion it jarred upon his feelings from some inexplicable reason. Why was it that she was haunted by fears of being less happy in the future? He asked himself that question, and was at a loss for an explanation. Since their marriage, a fortnight before, her character had provided him with a curious study. There were moments when her beauty and calm serenity rendered her irresistibly fascinating, but there were also moments when her slavish desire to carry out his slightest wish irritated him immeasurably. With a pang of disappointment he had already realised that companions, in the truest sense of the word, they could never be. Her apparent fear of differing from him, and the monotonous manner in which she therefore con- curred with all his suggestions, negatived any possibility of a pleasant interchange of thought. The desire to please him and to do his will un- questioningly dominated all her actions. But for a man of Dennis's independence of spirit, there was something inexpressibly depressing in the sight of a beautiful young creature reduced to a dead level of subservience.

Of one thing, however, he was absolutely sure— and that was that she loved him intensely. "I thought women always wanted plenty of change," he said, anxious to carry on the con- versation. "If to-day were to last for ever, I don't see where the change would come in. Do you not care for change and variety, Grace?" "Yes—oh, yes But then, you see, trouble and misery so often go hand-in-hand with change." "I don't think that; and it seems to my mind a miserable view to take of life. Change is the centre-point of all the pleasures of existence. If I imagined my days were to be played out to a continuous and never-changing routine, I should give up all idea of ever enjoying myself agaifi. Why do you fear the future? " She started, and turned very pale. "It is difficult to say," she answered; then added, as if anxious to change the topic of con- versation: "I am looking forward to going home. I have never had a comfortable home before—at least, not since I was capable of noticing my sur- roundings." "I gave the furnishing people carte blanche, up to a certain figure, so I suppose we shall find everything looking tolerably homelike when we return. How many servants shall we have to keep? " "How many did you wish to beep? "I have never given the matter a moment's thought. You must settle all that yourself." There was a lost look in Grace's face. She felt as incapable of assuming the reins of domestic government as an average schoolgirl, possibly more so.

"I know very little about housekeeping," she said hopelessly. "Naturally you don't know much. You will learn by experience, as half the married women do —so I suppose. It is a matter in which I cannot give you any advice." They were just entering the town, and neither spoke again until they had alighted at the hotel and were in their rooms. - .
Then Grace began, in a hesitating, nervous voice :
•--- • "Dennis, I dread the future because there is something I ought to tell you—and—oh! but I am afraid."
"Afraid of what ? " he asked.

"Of what you might say." "I was not aware that I had ever spoken to you in a manner that could cause you to be afraid of me." There was a slightly sarcastic ring in his voice. "However, if it is of any comfort to you to know that I have not the least doubt I shall say very little—whatever the secret may be—you can have that comfort. One would imagine I was in the habit of swearing at you, by the way you shirk saying what you have on your mind." "Oh, no, Dennis; you are always kind—always considerate."

"And the way you propose to reward my kind- ness and consideration is by being afraid to speak out frankly. Your conduct is inexplicable, Grace." He spoke bitterly, with the bitterness of a man who has striven to act a noble, self-sacrificing part, ana realises that disappointment is in store for him . "God knows I have done my duty," he ex- claimed. "Come, tell me, Grace," he added, assuming an authoritative manner, "what this secret is. Remember, there should be no secrets between man and wife."
But Grace uttered no word in response. "Will you not speak? Why did you tell me that this secret existed, unless you had decided to let me know what it concerned? "

"Forget what I said," she pleaded. "It is of no use your knowing. It does not matter to you now. It is all past." "Do you imagine you can put me off in this manner, after raising the most horrible suspicions in my mind ? " he asked indignantly. "If my wife possesses some secret which she thinks I ought to know, but which she fears would annoy me greatly, then, at. all hazards, she should let me hear it from her own lips, not run the risk of my hearing it from another's." "I4—spoke impulsively," was the only answer.

"Tell me !—I insist on your telling me ! " Then, almost in a whiiper, he added : "Are you free. from complications with other men ? " "Yes!" she cried, looking up frankly into his face. "You are the only man that 1 have over loved—the only one. "That is enough," he said, interrupting her. "It is at least satisfactory to lino* that my wife has not a dark past." The blood rushed into Grace's cheeks as she realised to the full extent what her husband's remark had inferred.

"I wish I had not spoken," she murmured. wish to Heaven you had not ! " he echoed fervently, "unless you were prepared to go fully into the matter. Not that I wish to know your secrets if you do not wish to tell them to me, I have purposely avoided talking of your home and your people, fearing you might imagine I wanted to hear about them; and from the moment you became my wife I wished your past life to be a sealed book. If, after all I have said, you insist on maintaining silence "—here he spoke more quickly, but at the same time more emphatically— "then, Grace, you will make me look upon our marriage very differently to what I have ever done before. Come, speak! What is this secret that you fear will ruin your happiness ? " "I did not say it would ruin my happiness, Dennis," she said faintly; "I only said I dreaded the future."

"Dreaded the future! Is not that practically the same thing? Be sensible. Tell me frankly what this trouble is that you said I ought to know. You can rely on my taking a lenient view of the matter. It belongs to the past. It cannot be undone. Does it concern your father as well as yourself ? "
"A little—but, oh! I cannot tell you now--" She broke off abruptly and buried her face in her hands.

"I am afraid you have not much courage," he said, trying to conceal how annoyed he was at her wife not trusting him. After a short pause he added : "When next your conscience prompts you to make a disclosure, I hope you will .decide to speak out boldly." "You are not very angry with me, Dennis 2" she asked with a sob.

oh, no," he answered; "yet you can't imagine [am exactly pleased or gratified. People do not Ls a rule stand in awe of me, and it strikes me as :onspicuously strange that my wife does. What induced you to begin telling me about this secret, ind then to break off and end by absolutely telling ne nothing, baffles my comprehension. I hadn't the remotest hankering to know any of your tocrets ; but when you tell me, in a inysterious voice, that there is something I ought to know, which you happen to know and I don't, and end )y letting me know nothing—well, you can't expect ne to be pleased ; and I certainly am not." With these words he abruptly left the room. "I ought--I ought to tell him lOh 1 but r :annot ! " she murmured to herself in an abjectly niscrable voice.
(To bo contiosed.)
HE ONLY IHOTTOIIT HE KNEW

DANTE spoke of Aristotle as "the master of those that know." And he did know, or thought he did, a great variety of things. He wail of an inquiring disposition and always trying to get hold of some of Naturo's hard facts. He put together a Ict of dogmas that ruled t world for ages, yet there wa3 not a teaspoonful cif truth in the entire combination. The shores of the past are sbrewn with the wrecks of scientific theories—those of this famous man with the rest. Taking a sweeping glance around him he discovered, or thought Le did, that there were exactly four elenlents—fire, air, earth, water, Fire and air, he said, have a natural motion upward ; earth and water downward. He asserted that the tendency of light bodies to rise and of heavy bodie to fall is inherent. Thus a thistledown ascended be- cause, like the tendency of dogs to bark, it " was its nature to." And when a brick got loose from a chimney top sad fell with a whack on the ground ,It was because of something "inhennt" in the brick. All of which must have been very cheery and enlightening to ths thinkers and the people of his day. He knew absolutely nothing about any fundamental law of Nature, yet nide versifies were founded on Aristotle. He commanded men's convictions. To-day every Intelligent person knows the philosophy of this ancient scientist to have been the sheerect stuff and nonsense. Yet, for suggest- ing a doubt as to the truth of it, Galileo was hissed at Florence; and Copernicus waited in silence thirty years before ha dared publish his book which expased and re- futed it.

From these considerations we perceive that it is net near so easy to " know " things as these old-time intel- lectual autocrats supposed it to be. Blunder as they did about the character of the world they lived in,they were still more deeply In the dark as to how their own bodies were made, and the way they performed their wonders' What sort of vital machinery was boxed up inside of their skins they bad no more notion than a Hottentot has of the integral calculus. All the same we are not quite at liberty to poke fun at those antique men of scienee,much less to blame them. For everything isn't settled yet by a good deal. Now an then we strike something that feels like bed rock, and when we do it is an acquisition to be thankful for and to hold on to. The predominant influence of the food system in the human boey over all its functions is one of those bet- torn truths. With all his wonderful physical and mental nature and powers man is nothing more or less that the product of the food he eats. Aristotle did not know thie but we do. And out of our knowledge of it proceed all correct and successful methods et preserving health. prolonging life,and combating disease. It follows that strengthand longevity signify continued good diges- tion,and that disease and death grow rank on the pois- oned soil called Dyspepsia. How the latter is treated nowadays is shown by the following illustration. "For several years," says a correspondent," I have been subject to severe attacks of indigestion. After meals I had great pain at the chest and sides, also a swollen feeling as if my clothing was too tight. I was troubled with wind rising into my throat. Every now and again I had attacks of windy spasms which gave me intense pain. I lest much sleep at night, and had I sinking feeling as if I had no power to walk about. I saw a doctor and took medicines, but got ne better. Three years ago I read about Mother Seigel'. Curative Syrup and began taking it. Soon I found very greet relief, the medicine dispelling all the wind and enabling me to eat without having pain. Since that time I have kept Mother Seigel's Syrup in the house as a family medicine, and we need no other doctor, for it keeps no In good health. I have recommended it to all my friendO and it has done a wonderful amount of good. For the benefit of others I Rave my consent to your Publishioll this statement. (Signed) (Mrs.) Eliza Higgs, 189, Wellfield-road, Streatham, London, August 4th, 1897.' When we succeed in curing dyspepsia, at least to a reasonable certainty in the great majority of cases, W shall have accomplished a result incomparably more beneficial to man thau any which has flawed front any art or soience ministering merely to our comfort and convenieuce ; for this is the disease which wastes and weakens the nations. Other ailments under various names grow out of it, as poisonous weeds grow in the stuck acd no ire of a festering swamp. The man or woman who prepares a genuine remedy for dyspepsia will be a greater. beaafactor to his fellows than than were any and ell the speculative philosophers for the set thousand years. A THREE HOURS' SITTING. A meeting of this Council was heldin the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, Warrington,on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Wright) presided, and there were also present—Alderman Fairclough (deputy Mavor),Aldermen Sutton, Francorabailack- hurst, and Hutchinson; Councillors H.Roberts,F.R. Roberts, John Roberts, Shaw Green, William Pier- point, Cannell, Plumpton, Smethurst, Longton Ben- nett, Evans, Ellison, Burton, Furness, Tinnion,Pea- cock, Grace, Jolley, Rogers, Shillcock, Wilkinson, Heaton, and Lee, with Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr. Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk),Mr. J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Mr. T. Longdin (borough surveyor),Mr.Gornall (medical officer),lllr. W. S.llaydock (gas engineer)._
TUE AUDITORS.
The MAYOR repor-te-(-1 -ttli;;;n-o-p-Plsed re-election of Messrs. Harrison and Bolton as elective auditors,and said that be appointed Councillor A. Bennett to be Mayor's auditor.

THE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS. The MITOR also referred to the election of Alderman Francomb, Mr. Frederick Monks, and Councillor Pier. point as county councillors. (Hear, hear.) He was sure that in them they should have three gentlemen who would look after the interests of the b )rough, and he congratulated Councillor Pierpoint on being one to make Up the number. (Hear, hear.) THE COST OF THE STREET LIMPS. The Street Improvement Committee recommended that the plan showing the line of frontage in Dial-street St. Anstireadane, Lower end of Bridge-street on the east side, and Friars' Gate be signed and deposited. There Was also the following item on the Committee's minutes: jeint meeting of the Gas Committee and Street Im- Movement and Lighting Committee was held to consider the terms upon which new mains should ate laid for Street lighting. It was stated by the Gas Engineer that there was a loss of 83. per lamp per annum on ordinary street lights. It was ultimately decided that if the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee would pay the actual nett cost of gas for street lighting, that all future extensions of mains and the provision of lamp pests should be made at the cost of the Gas Committee. Alderman Sorrow, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the first resolution referred to the system of fixing lines of frontsege which had been acted upon in various parts of the town. With reference to the meet- ing betweer the Gas Committee and the Street Improve- Ment Committee the statement in the minutes did not bind the Street Improvement Committee in any way. It was simply put there with the view of eliciting the Opinion of the Council on the question. The opinion of the majority of the Street Improvement Committee was that there should be notincrease in the rates of the borough but that,on the other hand, the Gas Committee 3 should continue to provide them with lamps at the same cost they were paying nose, or, in fact, that they Should do something more and make the lamps free as was done in many oth.r towns. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BLACK:BM:ST seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor Serzercuese asked in reference to the street frontages, whether there was going to be another pur- chase of property to widen the street in St. Austin's- lane. The MAYOR : We aro age presen only defining th. line of front- at the t time. Councillor SMETHURST : I think it is quite time we put our foot down in buying land to widen streets. He thought it would be better to confine themselves to im- provements in the centre of the town,and he considered the shop in Hnreemarket-street at the end of Lyme-st. should be pulled down as it made a dangerous corner Where there had been many accidents. Councillor SHAW GREEN said he had expected some reasons which induced the Gas Departmeut to make the Suggestions as to the lamps. In his opinion there were no reasons that could be given in favour of the proposal to increase the charges for the lamps, but, on the con- trary, he thought the Gas Department, Instead! of asking for higher prices, was in a position to give and ought to give a substantial sum in aid of the borough. In answer to Councillor GRACE, the MAYOR said £2 er ;anon was nele for the °Molnary street lamps. Councillor H. ROBERTS sup orted the suggestion that the minute be referred back. n He thought he should he able to eehmit figures later o in the evening to show that the Gas Committee was making a very substantial and very handsome profit and that the Corporation thould be receiving some benefit from it. The DSPUTY-MAYOR said they were net asking for an increased charge on the old lamps, but only whoa the street Improvement Committee asked them to lay new mains in new districts, and they were entitled by Act of Parliament to charge eight per cent noon this outlay. Councillor Femme said he believed the Gas Commit• toe wanted to charge £2 81. 4d. for all lamps. The DEPUTY-MAYOR: Nothing of the kind ; it is only in new districts where this increased charge is to be made. Councillor newness said they wanted b charge the ac- tual cost per lamp which is £2 8;. per anntun.The Street Improvement Committee would have to pay £BOO more Per annum which meant almost exactly a penny in the £on the rates. For his part, he should be prepared to Pay that if the Gas Committee could see its way to re- duce the price for gas. Councillor GRACE complained that the Gas Committee had not erected many lamps which had been ordered in litteets where mains were already laid. He thought I%,.arrington was very much beleiud other towns in the Ihting of the streets. r, COMRCIIInT TINNIOM, speaking as a member of the Gas Z°Thrnittee, said that committee had been asked to lay ''Sins in new streets regardless of the fact that there WOuld he no customers for gas in those streets. The "remittee had therefore asked that the Street Improve- Itlent Come-three should he responsible for eight per aent on the outlay. If the irrest lamps cost the Gas ‘'ornmittee 8; 41. more than they received, why should the -Y go on giving the Street Improvement Committee criPso eight and fnurn.rinne Counciller SHAW GREEN : Well,whv thouldn't they? Councillor TINNION said the Gas Committee should at least have all the credit for it. As long as the money ealows back to the town's pocket it did not matter two- enlace. Alderman Sterroe sail he would withdraw the entry in the minutes that was the ERMA of that discussion. Councillor PIBRPOINT RAid Alderman Sutton could not withdraw it without the permission of the Council, and be was, therefore, rather premature. Councillor LONOTON did not think the GAR Committee
cared mneh aa lqnz.aq it wal known that they were Los-

_ leg MO a year in the lighting of the streets. Councillor PLUMPTON wanted to know how it was that the Gas Committee had only now discovered that the Street Improvemnnt Committee was not paying the full Cost of the lamps. Mar did they come to the conclusiost that they were losing on each lamp? Sometimes street hums were not lit when they ought to be lit. He thought this was not the time for an increased charge for gas. „ COUUCillor PIERPOINT said FYI had, fortunately or un- fortunately as they might look at it,property in the area he had recently hen added to the borough, and oe charged the Gaa Committee with not having carried out the promise it made in order to induce him to give his vete in favour of extending the borough. The Town PIO, Park, and Baths Committee sub- mitted a report prepared by Mr. A. G. BarlOw,the baths superintendant, showing that the total number of bathers for the year ending 31st December. was 53,315, as against 48,353 1898, an increase of 4,982. The com- mittee also recommended that application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of £7OO for the purchase and laying out of the Queen's Gardens. Councillor Da. CANNELL said the Baths receipts had exceeded the estimate made at the beginning of the season by £3O or £4O. The head gardener had laid a plan beFore them for the laying out of Queen's Gardens. The committee required sanctinn from the Local Government Board to borrow £700.£200 of which would be spent on the purchase, and £5OO in laving the gardens out. He thought they would he able to get 20 or 25 years in which to repay the money. Councillor HEATON seconded the adoption of the minutes. .

Councillor F. R. ROBERT 3 said he had not seen the plan, but he would like to know whether the committee intended to remove the unsightly high railinys which surrounded the gardens at the present time. It seemed to him that they detracted from the appearance of the grounds, aryl he would suggest lower railings, or perhaps what would be far better, stone piers with iron chains. The MAT R: We cannot remove them under the terms of purchase. _

Councillor GIVICE called attention to the fact that there were 9,746 bathers in the second class plunTe bath, and r-ferred to the very limited accommodation pro- vided. He did not think the working classes could afford sixpence for the first class plunqe bath, and hs suggested that the first-class plunge bath might be thrown open after six o'clock on certain evenina., and the pries reduced to 31 fie thought that if such a course were adopted, there would be a large increase in the number of bathers. (Rear, hear.) Councillor LONEITON said the gardens seemed to be Planned out very nicely. hut he would like to see a fountain in the centre. This was an opportunity for some generous townsman to come forward and present one to the town.

He thought £5OO an extravagant sum to spend on the Gar- dens,

The MAYOR thought the suggestion of Councillor Grace was worthy the consideration of the committee. With reference to Councillor Pierpoint's observations,he might say that it did not necessarily follow that the committee was going to spend £5OO. Cluncillor CANNETL said the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee had nothing to do with Victoria Park. That was in the hands of the General Purposes Commit- tee. With reference to the Baths, he pointed out that the attendance at the second class plunge bath repre- sented ablut 40 per day. It was only crowded on Satur- days and then principally by boys.Councillor Grace had compared the first class bath with others in the coun- try but be could say that their first-class bath Was the cheapest in England. THE NEW POLICE BUILDIN./ 3. OPPOSITION TO TEE BARRACKS SITE. •

The General Parpeees Committee recommended that the old barracks in Arpley-street be selecte i as the site for the prepesed new police preneis).s., The Mare* Raid he would not inove,as W4llllig custom the minutes of this committee, as he did not approve of them in their entirete, Alderman BIACSIIIIRST moved, and Alderman FAIR.. moon seconded, the adoption of the minutes. C editor Timms said a deputation waited upon him that evening and asked him to present to the Council a petitien against the resolution adopting the old barracks as a site for the proposed new police buildings. The petitioners were the property owners and residents of St. Austin's Ware, and particularly in that portiou of the ward where the old barracks were situate I, and they asked that the buildings should not be erected on the proposed site, on the ground that the adj scent property would be deteriorated thereby. There were over 240 names appe vied to the petition, and he theught those people constituted . the flower of the townspeople. (Laughter). They all resided or had property in St. Austin's Ward. Fla believed that the site had been selected chiefly because of its size, and because it was adapted porhaps more than any other site to the require. tnents of the Homo Office. That was the only qualification it poseessed,but it was outweighed by many rii.olueheoi. tions.ln the first piece the barracks were n tin ass itral position, and the seems enacted in the inamediaLe ueivh- , bonrhood of is police court were not such as should be introduced into that portion of the ward. Re should like to know the average number, of prisoners weekly past five years at Warrington, as he failed te see for an acre and a quarter of land. He duritnhge ?ca m t ? understood that it was intended to have four out-stations —one at Sankey Bridges, Latchford, Manchester-road, and Winwiek-road, r zspectivey. The poice station shotid be iaty, was T)wn.taiii. placed rover the source of supply, and the proper as it had all the necessary 1p qtlalifiCitiong. He was a ware that someone must have a police court in their midst, but he did not see why it should be placed in that part of theßerough which rarely supplied a single prisoner to the Police Court. He moved, as an amendment, that the minutes referring to the selection of the old barracks as a site for the new police station be not c 'armed. If they adopted the Town. hill site they might have a large and comprehensive scheme by purchasing the whole of the property in that neighhourheod. There was no reason why the Council should go on with the scheme proposed simply because Sir Herbert Croft, H. 51. Inspector, was coming to Wet- rington on Wednesday. It would not matter as long as the subject was under consideration. Proceeding,Coun- cillor Tinnion remarked that he did not think the It acres would be insisted upon. The MAYOR: That is the requirement of the Home Office. They might be asked to accede to a smaller site,

, Cluncinor TIN/OXON (continuing),said it was very pro- bable that three-quarters of an acre veould be sufficient. He appealed to the gouncil on behalf of the inhabitants of St. ,Austin's ward that they would not inftint upon them the unfortunate element of a Police Court. He also appealed on behalf of the large number of school child- ren who fregnented the ward, and who would be the eye-witnesses of eights which it WAS undesirable that they should see. if the Police Court were built there. Flo hoped that another site would be selected,and that this " terrible " thing would not be thrust upon the inhabi- tants of St. Austin's ward. (Hear, hear). Councillor FURNESS seconded the amendment, and said the Council had no right to rush the matter. The only reason the Council had for adopting the Barracks site was that it was suitable so far as the site went, but he did not think that was sufficient to justify thorn in spending £15.000 or £20,000 on a police station at the place proposed. He would else like to remind the Council that they had there a Technical Institute, and the interest of the money they had paid for that place was being repaid to them by the Technical Institute. If they tookfthe building for a police station they would be invelved ire the expenie of building a new building for technical instruction purposes which would mean a mat- ter of fifteen to twenty thousand more. The Street Im- provement Cernmittee had spent elese upon £6OO in purchasing old property on Town-hill. and it seemed te him that for the next four or five years the purchasing of property would have to go on, but if they adopted Councillor Tinnion's suggestion he thought they might at one fell swoop take the whole lot in. He believed it would be an admirable site for the police station. , Even if it cost more money, they would be plid by the en- hanced rateable value of the property which would be built surrouniine the police station, and they would be carrying out an improvement in Buttertnirket-at. that was very much desired. If the Barracks site were fie- lected,the Council would first have to take into consider- ation the advisability of building a Technical Institute. '

. _ .. Councillor BoirroN considered the subject one of the most implrtant which had been brought before the 11 Council, and it demanded their most serious considera- tian before they adopted It. The site of the old barracks was too far from the centre of the town, and it would be very inconvenient for the police to take their pri- soners there, besides which the property owners htd a right to some ceneideration. Police stations exerted an influence for good in the neighbonrhood in which they were situated, but such influence would be altogether wasted in the neighbourhood suggested. Councillor H. Roirtave said he should support the minutes for the same reasons as they were proposed in committee. He would, however, like to gay that a petition representing the opinions of a large section of the population was entitled to great respect and every consideration. Ile found that the petition not only con- tained the names of a large number of property ewners and residette bat also the names of people who were not property owners and net ratepayers. There were also signatures of people on the petition who lived at ' such a distance from the site of the building that by no conceivable process could they be held to be prejudiced in the slightest degree by the erection of a police court at the old barracks. In confirmation of that statement he might say that several lived in Cairo-st., Bridge-st.,Friars'-gresn, Suez-st,, and Egypt-st. With regard to the suggestion that property would be depre- ciated, he respected the opinion of the property owners, but he thought they were entirely mistaken in their fears. He had only to quote the fact that in Birkenhead the police court and Town Hall combined were in the residential portion of the town, fronted by a large amount of property of infinitely more value than any property in any of the streets mentioned in the peti- tion.

CO:Manor TINIVON : " Question." Councillor ROMMTS (continuing) said ho thought hiS knowledge ef the value of property was as good as C,ormillor Tinnion's, and he had been to Birkenhead within a recent period and had seen the property and its contiguity to the police station. He was, therefore, able to speak as one having Quthority. He admitted at once that the barracks was not by any means an ideal site. (seer. hear.) It was only because they were " in a cleft stick" that he was there to support it. The Watch Committee had from time to time considered various sites. and enly a few days ago they took the members of the Council round and sliomed them four or five possible sites, most of which were rejected at once owing to the fact that their site was not sufficieet for the purpose. He took it for a fact that the Hems Offile req.] ired that an acre and a quarter should be provided, and that they would rifuse to sanction a plot of land less than that size. The Home Office knew their requirenunts better than the Council did. That being the case, they were confronted with the difficulty that suitable site were consequently, very small in number. Personally he should he delightedlo se a police court erected on

Town-hill. !jut they had to cut their coat according to MIMI cloth. Be was told by the Surveyor that the Town- bill site wont I oost £23,006 and the buildings would cost 'aihr £lsooo. Warrington could not afford to spend £40,000 on p dice buildings. We wanted other things far rn -ire than a police cmrt. (Hear, hear.) Many of them w r able to remember the time when the old barracks wee used y the Militia. People built property there, and continued to build,despite the scenes that took place a', tria-s and wadi, in his opinion, were far worse than ty num which would take place when the Police Court w ire quilt there. He had not the slightest hesitatiota in

xoressine the opinion that there would be no deprecia- If property by the erection of a handsome building seitabl, fir the purposes of a police station. There was the fur ;ler adventage that the buildings were their own t “int i y could t;ke immediate peseassion. He be lieved 'l9 barracks could be continued in use as a Tech- n mai lestitute for some years to come. (Hear, hear.) he ditfi natty ab mc the site not being central would be go; ever by the erection of bridewells at Sankey Bridges and Fr Winwick-roal, Latchford, and Manchester-road, which w a, I his eq ripped with every appliance to deal with a refrac;ory individuel. There was also another matter which should not be overlooked. Ambulances were new being largely used for the removal of prisoners arid he did n oeiree why they could not be introduced into Warrington. Caunciller FINNIC:ON : It IS too costly. Councillor ROMIRTS : It is an itom of cost which no one would object to. If there was a more central site at a reasonable cost and to be had within reasonable time he would support it, but as there was no such site, sad as the suggested one afforded the facility for immedi- ate entrance he should support the proposal. Councillor Beezierr considered that the argument of the cleft stick with which Councillor Roberts opened was an unfortunate one. He hesitated to admit that the Corporation were in a position that they must accept a site simply because S r Elerlocrt Croft was coming on Wednesday. (Hear, bear.) If the Inspector saw they were in earnest, and they asked for another week or two Co consider the question, he would not take any ac- tion. lie (the speaker) thought the matter had been rushed somewhat, as it was only the last month or so that it he I been before them. At the same time he recogniz .4 that there was a good deal in all Councillor Roberts had said. Town-hill was obviously more con• tail, and if they applie t the barracks to the purposes of a police station they would, despite what Councillor Roberts said, have to provide a further !melding for a 'Fechaicallaititute and it would prevent any possibility of seeing the Wracks used as a cattle market. ("Oh, Oh') He had never ceased to regret the decision of the Corporatioe in rejecting the peoposal to establish a cattle ins - k3t there. The old barracks was not central, but he Omitted that it might be as time went on. Al lemma Streroor supported the amendment. He considere 1 that the prayer of the petitioners was a most reason able one,that was to keep that part of Warrington as pleastat and attractive as possible,so that the inhabi- tants might take advantage of it in their walks. He still thought the land adjoining Bath-street was the meet de- sirable site,and he agreed with the suggesiion that had bees thrown out,that they should form a comprehensive scheme for concentrating their municipal offices and pablic buildings as much as possible. Councillor Roberts was somewhat inconsistent in his arguments In refer- ence to the Barracks. First of all he objected altogether to the site that the Watch Committee suggested be- cause--- Couneelor li ROBERTS Mr. Mayor, I beg to rise to a point of order. lithe Alderman in order in introduc- ing a discussion which occurred some weeks age, and %swab boo n ) reference at all to the minutes before this meeting ? • Alderman Surroor was about to speak when Councillor Rosman said: lam asking the Mayor, not you. Alderman SUTTON L., It does not matter who you are asking' jam telling you. (Laughter.) The 'duos: Alderman Sutton has a perfect right to make use of this explanation. Councillor ROBERTS said he should make the explana- tion he made in committee as to the difference between the Bath-street site and the old barracks site. Alderman Surroe : You can bring any argument to Stilt your purpose at any time. Councillor ROBEaTS : lam able to give my opinions on any question. Alderman SUTTON : Ido not say—. Couneillor ROBERTS: Well, just be careful what you do say. Alderman SurroN : I did not question your capabili- ties. • Councillor ROBBRTS : You questioned my honesty. Alderman Surroor : I ant simply stating the facts. I say you are inconsistent in your remarks to-night and the remarks you previously made. Councillor RORBRTS I say you are utterly incapable of understanoiag the English language if you make any such statement. The aim a (to Alderman Sutton) : Will you kindly %Meese your remarks to the chair ? Alderman Surma : Well, do not let ma have any in- terferense from Councillor Roberts, Cmincillor ROBERTS Well, then, do not say anything that is not true. Alderman Sorrow contended that Councillor Roberts said that if the police buildings were erected near the Town Hall, they would affect the comfort of those who come into the park. Couecillor Ronsars : I didn't. It was an entirely different argument. Alderman FRINCOMB : That site is not on the milt:dos and should not be referred to. Alderman Surrotr : We have been told to-night by Councillor Roberts that the police 'station would not affect the inhabitants in the slightest degree. I am try- ing to show his incensistency. Councillor Roesees : I said it would not affect the depreciation of property. 1 protest against words being put into my in oath which I have never uttered either on this occasion or any previous occasion. Alderman SUTTON : lam simply stating the truth. I think I am not setting the chair at defiance. The MAYOR : I don't approve of their; interruptions. Alderman Surroe : I have said nothing to which ob- jection can be taken. I don't think Councillor Roberts need be upset about it. Councillor ROBERTS : Thank you. Alderman SUTTON : You cannot have your way al- ways. (Laughter) Centinuing, be said he was net in favour of the Town-hill site at present, because they would have to pay a large sum of money for the pur- chase of property in the neighbourhood,and it was quite true that the Local Government Boardldistinctly stated that they ought to have at least an acre and a quarter of land. He contended that the Bath-st site met all the requirements. It was owned by the Corporation and they could have immediate possession. A petition like that which Councillor Tinniou hscl presented should be respected and he must say that ne preferred the Bath- st. site. Ceuncillor Peyote-roe said he had listened to the various speeches which had been mede,but he could not find anything new in the arguments raised against the use of the barracks site. The County Court was built in the vicinity,and those attending that place were quite as bad as those attending, the police court. (Laughter) Couacillor Dr. CetriaLL : Worse. (Renewed laugh- ter) Councillor TINNION But we don't want both. Ceuncillor PLIMPTON (continuing) said that the old barracks was the best site in the town. It appeared to him that the people of Bt. Austin's Ward were ready to object to everything. (Laughter.) The representatives of the ward were no doubt doing their duty in the action they were takleg: and it would be of service to them on another occasion. (Renewed laughter). He thought they could very well afford to let it stop at that. When the site was proposed for a cattle market it was said that the cows would be dangerous to the school children, but if the police station were there they would be able to protect them. (" Vote, vote.") Councillor PIIIRPOTNT was Sorry to prevent the vote being taken, but he thought the discussion was of such importance that it Should not be snuffed out. (Hear, bear.) The M&YOR : 1 dent want to stifle the discussion. Councillor PIBRPOINT proceeded to say that be had come to the meeting with an open mind, and the present was the first discussion he had heard with reference to the new police station. Councillor H. Roberti; was one of the cleverest advocates they had in the Council Cham- ber, an he had that evening made a most admirable speech, but the worst of it was that he prefixed it with an observation that was rather distracting to his (Coun- cillor Pierpoint's) mind, namely, that he aporoved of the site as a matter of urgency because Sir Herbert Croft was coming to the town en the morrow. Therefore, in his opinion, Councillor Roberts had put his weakest point first. The MAYOR: It was chiefly on account of area. Councillor PIIIRPOINT, continuing, said that although he had come into the room with an open mind he was now in tile position that he had not been able to form an opinion either for or against the scheme, and he thought he should have to vote for Councillor Tinnion's amend- ment.

Alderman Fasnows said he was of the opinion of Councillor t. Roberts, that if they could not get a site without Spending £20,000 for old property they should select the old barracks. But, on the other hand, if they could get a site without the area being an acre and a quarter. he did not see why ths discu-saion should not be adjourned for another week and a deputation wait upon Sir Herbert Croft to see if a less quantity of land would suffice. If se he would go in for another site. n it was found that an sore and a quarter were necessary he should go in for the old barracks. Alderman Btackuostav said he had been a member of the Watch Committee, and had bad some little experi- ence about the si:es which bad been pointed out all over the town, but he could net quite decide whether the old barracks was the best place or not. At the same time, he lived that the Council would that evening onoe for all decide the matter. (Cries of " Vote, vote.") Councillor TINN2CON : Is it absolutely essential that we most have not less than an acre and a quarter of land?

The M&YOR That is so. The Home Offios demands it for the number of police we have and the population of the town. I am just reminded that the police cells at Blackpool cover an area of an acre and a quarter. Councillor Timms It is the only town in Lancashire

that does. The Mayon: They have a less population than we have. (Cries of "Vote, vote.") Councillor GRACE would like an evplanation given about the question of the acre and a quarter. Was that quantity ot land essential? He knew Birk-nhoad as well as anyone in Warrineton, and the p-slice t'uildinzs there, for a population of 155,000, and 140 policc.,with a bride. welt and three police courts and every convenience, did not stand on half an acre of land. Councillor H. ROBERTS: Nonsense. Councillor GRACE: lam not talking about the Town Hall.—(Cries of "Vote, vote.") The MAYOR : There appears to be a desire on the part of the members of the Council that we should now I come to a vote. Councillor SISETIIIIRST said that at the last meeting of the Council he mentioned a suitable site for a police station, and he would venture to do so again that even- ing. The site was in the neighbourhood of King-street, Flag-lane, and Golborne-street—a site which came into two main streets,and was within 20 yards of the whole- sale and retail market, and was also right in the centre of the town. They owned the largest portion of the property, and there was above an acre of land. The MAYOR ; There is not, Councillor Smethurst. Alderman Serrots : We have an acre and an eighth near the Town Hall. The voting was then proceeded with, with the follow- ing result : For the amendment, that the minutes of the com- mittee relating to tbe proposed site be not confirmed : Alderman Sutton ; Councillors Burton, Pierpoint, Fur- ness, Tinnion, Peacock, Grace, Rogers, Heaton and Lee —lO. Against: Aldermen Fairclough, Blackhurst, and Francomb ; Councillors H. Roberts, Dr. Cannel', Plump. ton, Longton, Evans, Ellison,F. R. Roberts, Jolley, Shill. cock, Wilkinson, and John Roberts-14. The MAYOR : The amendment is lost. Councillor TINNION proposed another amendment, and said he vreuld adopt the suggestion of Alderman Fran- comb, that the matter be deferred until after the visit of Sir Herbert Croft. Councillor LONGTON • IS that in order ? Councillor Tmistorr : Quite in order. The MAYOR: lam advised you cannot propose that. Councillor TnerrioN : Well, then, I will propose an amendment. I beg to propose as an amendment that Town-hill be selected as the site. Councillor LONGTON Is that in order? The MAYOR: No. Councillor LONG-CON : I think we had b:tter settle the matter to-night. Councillor TINNION : We are only considering one site. The MAYOR: The only course you can adopt is to pro- pose the adjournment of the Council. Councillor TINNION : Then I beg to propose the ad- journment of the Council. I do so for the reason that the matter has been made argent, largely because of the visit of Sir Herbert Croft on Wednesday. I propose the adjournment of the Council that the Watch Committee may see Sir Herbert Croft and ascertain whether it is essential that there should be an acre and a quarter of land. There has been word received from the Red-tape House Office that an acre and a quarter of land is neces- sary.

The MAYOR : We are not bound by any decision of Sir Herbert Croft, who has the supervision of the police cells. lam afraid we have to show more deference to the Home Office than to anyone else. Councillor TINNION : I propose the adjournment of the Council for a fortnight. The DEPUTY-MAYOR : This day 12 months. (Laughter.) Councillor TiNezote :If that date suits you it will suit ma. I thank yea for another. (Laughter.) Alderman SUTTON seconded the amendment for the adjournment of the Council for fourteen days, but on being put to the meeting it was lost by a large majority. Councillor TINNION D 1 you new rule that we cannot go en with any other scheme ? We shall have a town's meeting and a vote of the town. We are not at all satisfied. The MAYOR : Very well. Councillor Tnemos : We contend we have the best of the argument to-night. The MAYOR : Very well. Councillor Tinsion : We could have got 10,000 signa- tures. The minutes of the committee were then agreed to. PROPOSED REMOVAL OF GAS OFFICES. Conuncillor Saaw GREEN in accordance with notice moved "That a committee be appointed to consider the advisability of transferring the cash and book-keeping department of the Gas Works to Bank House,as it is cal- culated im save cost to the Corporation, and he a great convenience to the public. He said the suggestion that all the business of the town should be done in one cen- tral office was no new thing, as a great deal of trouble was given to ratepayers in having to go to Mersey-at. in order to give an address or pay a gas bill. There was no reason why all accounts should not be paid over one counter. He proposed that the following form the com- mittee :—Aldermen Fairclough and Bolton, Councillors Shaw-Green, Burton, and Shillcock. Councillor Trnmote seconded this proposal. Alderman FAIRCLOUGH said the Gas Committee had no objection to Bank House. The only thing was the want of room there. On the committee propesed there was only one member of the Gas Cornmittee,and he suggested that the matter should be dealt with by the Finance Committeee and the Gas Committee. This suggestion was agreed to. GAS COMMITTEE FINANCE. Councillor Henry Roberts had given notice of the follow- ing resolution that :—The Gls Committee be instructed to furnish a report to the Council showing: The amount of money charged in the cost of the manufacture of gas for (4. All renewals and repairs rendered necessary by ordinary wear and tear. (b). All renewals or replace- meats caused by any other circumstances (the CIMISOS of such renewals or replacements te be set out in the re- port). (e) All additions to plant, mains or buildings, temporary or permanent.—The report to cover the period from January Ist, 1890, to December 31st, 1897, and to show the cost separately for each year. It was however suggested that the consideration of this motion should be adjourned as the Council had now sat till nearly nine o'clock. Councillor H. Ronzwrs said he had taken considerable trouble in preparing what he had to say,but if the Coun- cil would undertake to keep him a qu ruin at the next Council meeting he should be satisfied. He moved the adjournment of the Council till the 15`h March. He ad- ded that be had figures there which it was important should be known. It was necessary that the policy of the committee should be disclosed. The Mason: I think you will have a fair hearing. In answer to the MATOft, Councillor H. ROBERTS said that he thought the matter was well worthy of a special meeting. Councillor Smivr GREEN seconded the proposal that the Council be adjourned till the 15th March. Councillor PIERPOINT Elek it that the Gas Committee were not afraid of the fullest consideratien. Councillor Hearott said he took it for granted from the insinuations that the Gas Committee bad done some- thing wrong. Councillor H. ROBERTS: Yea ; they have. The DEPUTY-MAYOR: They have done nothing except under the advice of their legal adviser. Colurnwcialsishld then age he o agreed that tn he 15 hatta special meeting of the March. THE MAYOR AND VVYCLIFFE CHURCH. A NEW DEPARTURE. The MAYOR said : It has been seggested to me on feealnlow townernen and t several o:casions that we might attend divine service at Wycliffe Church on the occasion of the re-openimr after cy° m attend. Paine d decorations. Therefore I purpose going there on Sun- day morning next, and I hope I shall pboessiabcl Ibt hys ehaaal lmal Fb Guardians, eo f tlyoueoaos.e v vgentlemenu i t nad SF show Wycliffe Church as much respect as We do the Church of England. (Hear. hear.) THE WIDENING OF BRIDGE STREET. At the conclusion of the business Councillor SHAW GREEN as Chairman of the Finance Committee proposed that the Council adopt two agreements made for the purchase from the Executors of the late John Tort and the Executors of the late Sarn.uel Sutton, of property be- longing to them in that portion of Bridge-street ached- uled to be widened. Alderman FAIR.CLOUGIS seconded, and it was unanim- ously agreed to.

div.head: SABBATH.
div.p: THE SABBATH.

This day is thine ; its hours, its all, A hesvenE impress bear; Father, our wand'ring steps recall That we its joys may share. Weary and worn with toil and pain, We hail this season blest: Now Love unbinds the six days chain, And gives the weary rest. Calm as the world around us lies. 0 may our spirit be; And, cloudless as the summer skies, The faith that looks to thee. And now Thy table, Lord, is spread, For all who feel their need : 0 let us hire Thy children's bread, On heavenly manna feed. Still, too, by Elm's sacred palm. The living water flows : And still in Gilead there is balm For human wants and woes. 0 may we drink otthese pure rifle, And all their virtues prove; While Jesus on each soul distils His healing balm of love. And, Lord, above these hills of time, From Pisgah's lofty brow ; We fain would scan a brighter clime, And see Thy glory now. Hail, blessed day! thou art to me A sunny spot on life's dark sea : A little isle around whose shore The surging billows break no more : Whose skies all cloudless, all serene, O'er-arch fair hills of living green' And healin streams, that still gmake glad. The poor, the weary, and the sad. Warrington. J. H. W. CLINDINNINC-.
