div.p: THE EXAMINER.
MARCH 4 h, 1598.
• THE subject of child labour was on Education. Wednesday brought prominently

under the notice of Sir Joule GOBST, the vice-President of the Council for Education, by a deputation representing import- ant educational and labour authorities. The ob- ject of the deputation was to urge the raising of the school age, or, at all events, to advocate the abolition of the "half-time " system and other exemptions from attendance at school, by which the education of English children is restricted. The importance of this question will not be minimised by any enlightened person. There is robably more talk at the present time in this country about foreign rivalry in trade than there has ever been before since manufacturing indus- tries became an essential part of the national life. The:cause of that, of course, is :not far to seek It is to be found in the continually increasing keenness of foreign competition in lines of trade which we had been trained to look upon as peculiarly British. The hith- erto despised foreigner is actually threaten- ing to get the upper hand in markets which used to be almost monopolised by our own merchants. There are no doubt many explana- tions that might be advanced to account for this trade revolution, but probably the most impor- tant of all is the fact that in those countries which are our most formidable competitors the education of the children is made more thorough and systematic every year. In such countries as Getmany and Switzerland the object aimed at above all others is the development of the facul- ties of the young; in this country some features of our educational system seem to have been specially devised for the purpose of discouraging and retarding education. Lord REAY, chairman of the London School Board and one of the depu- tation, pointed out to Sir Joao Goner that in some parts of England and Wales, children of ten were entirely exempted from school attendance. In other cases while still attending school the boys and girls were stunted by excessive work out of school hours. Another member of the deputa- tion mentioned the case of a child which, in addition to going five full days to school, worked sixteen hours on the Saturday and six and a half hours on the Sunday. Another school girl of nine years had to get up at four o'clock in the morning to wake the considerate working people of the neighbourhood in which she lived. These are no doubt extreme cases,but they are in some respects typical of a vast amount ef child labour that is still enforced in this country, and which is entirely inconsistent with the best development of either the mental or the physical qualities of the rising generation. The nalf-time system is meat preva- lent in parts of Lancashire and in the West Rid- ing of Yorkshire, and although it has now, we believe, been shorn of most of its worst abuses, it still is, or ought to be, out of harmony with the spirit of the present age. In his reply to the de- putation, Sir Joux Goasx made a decidedly despondent speech, though there is unques- tionably a large amount of truth in the arguments he uses. Sir Joule himself is, as every- one knows, a convinced educ ationist,and appears to be far in advance of any other member of the present Government in that respect. He evidently thinks that he and other education reformers are also in advance of the opinion of the country generally. He admits that many improve ments are needed, but he, in effect, asks from whence the motive power to effect these improvements is to come? As to the half-timers in Lancashire and Yorkshire, for instance, he points out that even the trade unionists in the distric ts where th system is in vogue are dead against any change. If, then, the working people themselves do not want , their children fully and efficiently educated, how can you expect politicians who depend upon work- ing men for their votes to attempt any rofor m which might only lose them their seats in the House of Commons ? Sir Jon Goan is of

opinion that views adverse to educa- tion are more widely entertained in this country than many people imagine. The territorial aristocracy of the country do not want the poor educated because it might lead them to think that they were just as well qualified as some of their "betters "to adorn a higher social sphere. Mr. JOBEPTI ARCH has described iu his autobio- graphy recently published how carefully the social distinctions were observed even at the sacraments in the parish church of his native village, and the numerous squires scattered over the country do not want that system disturbed if they can help it. Then, again, says Sir JOHN GORST, there are other elements in country districts adverse to education. The farmers do not want the mental faculties of the children of the labourers too finely trained, for in that case the growing crop of work- men might be disposed to revolt against the unin- telligent drudgery which was the fate of their fore- fathers. And, as a climax to all the rest, the labourers themselves do not value education at any very high rate. They would rather have the small earnings of their children, and therefore take their boys and girls from school at the earliest possible moment. It must, we are afraid, be admitted that there is a great deal of truth in all this, but on the whole Sir JOHN GORST paints his picture with rather too gloomy colours. There can be no I doubt that there has been a very marked advance in educational matters during the last twenty or thirty years,and we are much mistaken if the coun making tryakiisnot quietly and gradually but inevi- tablyup its mind to have some further improvements. Education is much more widely spread than it used to be, an 4 educated people are the people to appreciate the value of education.
Th Ship A more encouraging account of e Canal. the affairs of the Ship Canal

was given at Manchester CitY Council on Wednesday than has appeared for a long time. Six months ago the outlook was de* Pressing in the first half of 1897 the earnings of the canal had fallen below those of the previous half year, and that, in the opinion of many people, was decidedly ominous. It seemed to show that the traffic instead of steadily advancing had actually begun to decline. During the last six months of 1897 U .ere has, however, been a marked change for the better. While in the first half of the year there was a fall of £l,OOO, in the second there was an increase of no less than £20,000. This :large sum was made partly by an actual increase of revenue to the extent of £lO,OOO and partly by a decrease of expenditure by a similar amount. It is now predicted that the Canal Company will be able this year to commence the payment of In- terest on the Corporation loans which should give satisfaction to the Manchester ratepayers.

At Stockton Heath there is soma little effort s. ing made to persuade property owners into a com. prehension of the dangers. attending the use o

Privy middens, and the superiority in .sanitary and other respects of the modern water closet. Sanite- tion is making great strides all over the country', but its innovations and improvements are princi- pally confined to the towns, and the wise action of tha Stockton Heath Parish Council is one which should commend itself very strongly to similar bodies. Many of:onecountry parishes are in a de- plorable state as regards sanitary and all matter per- taining to healthy existence,but Stockton Heath 18 far removed from such a condition. Yet there ie room for improvement, and this fact being evident to the body having control of the affairs of the parish, steps are being taken in the direction indi° cated. It will, perhaps, strengthen their halide in such action if we quote a paragraph bearing directly on the matter, from the "British Medical Journal." This great authority seys It is astonishing how long some of our northern, towns have clung to such abominations as privi middens,and how tenaciously the property owner; adhere to the sanitary ideals of fifty years ago. During a recent apneal case before the Salford Hundred Sessions,Professor Del6pine mentioned ill evidence that he had found in two samples of earth collected by the sanitary inspector from crevices of the ashpit the bacilli of typhoid fever. Since tbe adoption of notification Dr. Crocker has bad 32.' cases of typhoid fever reported from houses with midden privies and only 25 f torn those with water closets."
ANNUAL POLICE INSPECTION AT WARRINGTON

At 10-15 on Wednesday morning Sir Croft, Bart, Inspector of Police forces for the Northern Division, visited Warrington and mad' his annual inspection of the borough police, at' Drill Shed, Bath-street. There were present on ....- half of the Corporation the Mayor (Alderman J. D. Wright), Alderman Fairclough (deputy mayor), - J. :a. Whittle eTown Clerk), Mr. Stanley Wilt'. deputy town clerk), r. John Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Mr. G. F. F. White (deputy magistrate' clerk) and Mr. I. enry Taylor (Police Court Mimic! ary). There were on parade, the Chief Constat (Mr. Luke Talbot) 5 inspectors,s sergeants, 45 co stables, total 56. The Chief Constable and Inspect Phillips put the men through their drill, which, may state is the latest code of infantry drill drawn up by the War Office. The various move ments were performed with a unity and precisioo which approached.a high standard and . .

much credit upon the instructor(lnspector Philli and the Chief Constable, Sir Herbert Croft DI made an examination of the clothing and accout merits of the men, which be found in thorougl- good order. The Rev. Cannon Msitland Wood, writing in the cur- rent number of the " Parish Magazine," says -.•—" if our people had half as much devotion to the service of God as they had to religious or secular amusements we should not find Mr. Grossmith with the Drill Hall crammed to the doors. nor Mr. Jude demanding for himself silver eollections, and apparently getting them in very un- propitious weather, whilst the House of God ii thinly attended, if a cloud passes over the sue or the streets are even a little damp. Any excuse or none seems sufficient to check devotion, but nothing is allowed to stand in th way of amusement. " Where your treasure is there will your heart be also."

ALLEGED THEFT OF & WATCH. William Johnson, a well-known character was re- manded on Friday, by Mr. F. J. Norman, at the Run- corn Police Court for a week on the charge of stealing a Waterbury watch from the Salt Works at Weston Point, the property of David Walker, an employ 6 at the works. It appeared that the prosecutor went to work about five o'clock in the morning, and hung his watch on a nail in the "hothouse.,' At 8-30 he saw the prisoner in the "hothouse," and at quarter-past nine ho found the prisoner had vim. He looked for his watch and found that had gone also. He gave information to the police, but as they had not been able to recover the watch. Johnson was remanded.

DEATH OF AN OLD RIINCORNIAN. The mortal remains of Peter Hindley aged 71 roars were committed Co their last resting place at the Run- corn Cemetery, on Monday afternoon. For a great many years deceased was an engine driver on the Holyhead line of the London and North-Western Railway,and was the man to make the trial trip through the tubular bridge at Menai Straits. He retired from the Company's service about 20 year, ago and sot up business in Run- corn as a general dealer. The Rev. C. W. L. Christien of St. Paul's Wesleyan Church, performed the burial service. _ .

Thee, consisted of president, I three vice-presidents, secretary, treasurer, organist, and accompanist, and five committees all having separate Iduties. The membership now stands at 150, and the brotherhood bids fair to do a good work. JOEN BUNYAN : ADDRRSS AT RUNCORN. Samuel Wright, (ex-President of the Free Methodist Conference, and the present pastor ef Bites- , mere-street Church), was delivered More the Elleensere- street Mutual Improvement Seciety on Friday evening by Mr. Joseph White. There was a large attendance, the chair being oecupied by Mr. James Scrag, who in a brief speech.expreesed the pleasure it gave him to pre- side over the meeting, which he felt sure would hear from Mr.Whire much that weuld interest and instruct them. Mr. White. who was received with cheers, then proceeded with his address.which was listened to with close attention, k short discussion followed, the mem- bers speaking in complimentary terms of the address, sad on the motion of the Rov.S.Wright.secoaded by Mr. James Turnbull a cordial vote of thanks was passed to Mr. White. _

div.head: RUNCORN BellOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BellOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the Runcorn School Board was held on Tuesday evening at the Town Hall,Runcorn, Mr. J. Pritchard (in the chair). There were also present the Rev. Canon Wood, the Rev. Father Gore, Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., F. J. Norman, J.P. E. Nilson, C. 0., and C. A. Timmins. The Clerk, Mr. Moss, was absent through illness.—The School attendance Committee re- ported that the scholars on the registers numbered 3,343 against 3.383 in the corresponding month of last year, decrease 40. The average attendance was 2,856 against 2.739, increase 117. The percentage of attendance was 85.4 being an increase of VS.—The tender of Mr. S. Coventry, of Runcorn, to supply the visitors' uniforms was accepted .It was decided to serve a precept for £B5O upon the overseers to meet the eapenses of the Board during the half year ending September 29th, 1898.

div.head: MINSTREL_ ENTHRTAINMENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MINSTREL_ ENTHRTAINMENT AT RUNCORN.

The Public Hall, Runcorn. was on Wednesday evening packed with an appreciative audience which had assem- bled to witness an entertainment by tile w(11-known local Charity Minstrel Troupe. Master Jack Rutter pleased the audience with his song" Mother's Darling " and was given an encore. He sang" Dick Whittington" in a nice style. The comic song entitled " Insurance Man" by Mr. W. H. Malings received the plaudits of the audience, as also did Mr. W. R. Davies' rendition of " Dollys Day Dream." The little Misses Kitty Rutter and Betty Jones delighted their hearers with the duet "You shan't play in our yard." They were accorded an encore, and repeated the duet. Other items in this half were songs by Mr. F. Crowther, Master Jack Rutter,Air. J. Casson, and Mr. J. Shingler. In the second half the artistes who distinguished themeelree were Miss Edith Jones, Mr. W. H. Malings,Mr. W. R.Davies, Misses bitty Rutter, P. Suett and Betty Jones, Mr. T. Kaight,Master Jack Davies, Mesers. H. Suett and J. Knight, Misses E. Suett, Eva Jones and Edith .Tones' Messrs. G. Casson, and F.Crowther. The children all took their parts in a manner which reflected great credit on their teacher, Mr. W. R. Davies. Mrs. Kenyon Davies was the con- ductor of the orchestra.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions,on Mmaday,before Mr. A. Thomas (chairman) and Mr. W. Timmins. John Wil- liam Moores, aged 12,was charged with breaking a win- dow in Halton-lane, the proderty of Thomas Bartlett— Frank Johnson, agent to Mr. Bartlett, stated that they had scores of window panes broken on this property by lads throwing atones. They were net content with damaging the windows, but they broke in the panels of doors, until at last they found it necessary to come he- Uwe the magistrates in order to try and prevent it—The Chairman said that on that occasion the defendant would he leniently dealt with. Be would have to pay the costs and the damage,a total of 8. But if there was a continuance of that sort of thing, they would have to deal more severely with the offenders.—Freelerick Edkins was summoned for disobeying an order made by the Bench requiring him to send his son Frank regularly to school. COMPLIMENTARY BANQUET.

On Saturday evening a complimentary banquet was given to eir John T.Brunner, Bart., M.P.,by Mr.Sarauel Taylor, J.P., C.C., and Chairman of the Urban Distriet Council of Runcorn,in recognition of his generous aid to Technical Education and other public objects in the town of Runcorn, in the large art room of the Technical Institute. Mr. Taylor presided and the guests were : Sir John T.Brunner, M.P.,Mesara.P.Speekman,J.F,C.C. J. W. Lightburu, J. Pritchard, D. Biabrown, J.Wilsoad. Jones, W. Collier, T. Dean, G. flevriet,W. Grice, Elorsefield, G. H. Kirkham, F. Wiswall and M. Sweetman, members of the Urban Ceuncil,M.L. Davies, J. R. Frith, W. Hankinson, J.Helt, E.Key, W.Moston,A. R. Norman, J.P, F. J. Norman, J.P, it. H. Posnett, R. RawLimon, J. Turabull, J. Turner,and Holland,members of the Technical Instruction Committee, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), J. Wilding (eur- veyor), M. Barker (consulting surveyor), J. D. Joao (librarian), T. C. Haddock (treasurer), Lawrensoa (headmaster sif the Secondary Day School), and Dr. McDougall medical officer of health)officials;ind Captain G. F. Ashton; Superintendent Okell„ Frank Jelnason, J. Frith, W. Frith, and J. T. Gordon(Runcorn"Examiner") C. Temkins ("Guardian") and F. Whalley (" Weekly News"). The tables had been beautifully and magnifi- cently laid oat by the Misses Taylor and Clara Taylor, and Mrs. James Frith. A small orchestral hand from Liverpool played selections during the evening. The waiters were supplied by Messrs. Biker of Chester. The Chairman proposed " The health of our guest,Sir John Brenner." He (the chairman), was quite safe he saying that they had not had a gentleman amongst them who had helped every worthy cause in Runcorn mere than Sir John had done. Some three years ago depression arose in Runcorn which placed the town in a very unfortunate position. A great number of works were practically closed, and, unfortunately, they ex- perienced a long and severe frost about the same time. they appealed to their friends locally and abroad, and he was quite sife in saying that had it not been for the great support they received from their friend Sir John Brunner a great number of people would have suffered. (Hear, hear.) About the same time the people of Runcorn—more particularly among the friendly socie- ties and trade societies of the town—were desirous of leaving A home for themselves. 'file question was mooted to Sir John Brunuer, and he generously came to the front and bought a building, and ha might say almost pulled it down and re-arranged it in euch a form that it had met the requirements of the town. (Hear, hear.) He was sure that for a long time to come those people who were deriving the benefit from that house would thank Sir John Brunner far his gift. (Rear, hear.) Then he (the chairman) came to the education question. They all knew that Sir John Brunner was a great educationist and he felt sure they would not have had that beautiful,and useful building in which they were now assembled if it had not been for the great support receieed from Sir John. (Flear,hear.) Be teld them in the first place he would help them if they would help themselves. He was very pleased to see that that offer nut all the ratepayers in Rune urn on their metal,and they did help th angel yes. (Hear,hear.) Sir John came forward nod fulfilled his promise. Subsequently he said " You have got a debt on your building of something like £1,401,700 raise £5OO and I will give you £500." (Applause.) They were fortunate in mekine their appeal in the Jubilee year. (Hear, hear.) Be (the chairman) appreciated the '97 Jubilee 50 times more than he appreciated that of 1887, and it was for this reason. They had an excuse to go to their friends. They bad an excuse to appeal from door to door, and they never had abetter response from the people. They succeeded in raising the £soo,and in the natural course of things they applied to Sir John Brunner to fulfil hie promise. To his (the chairman'e) very great surprise,and he was sure to the surprise of every man, woman, and child in Runcern who could understand the matter, Sir that ar Runcorn,hear, a Urbanap pl au Counciles. ) Raen d couldth the John sent them a cheque for £9BO, and thus treed the absusiuldreingsoirf jdoehbrit. ( people of the town thanked him very much for his gil t. He felt sure they were all satisfied Sir John Brunner had a big hearte (Applause.) and he asked them to drink to his health.

The toast was received with -enthusiasm the company singing "For he's a jolly good fellow." The Chairman then called upon Mr. Wilson to make a presentation of a portrait to Sir Jobe on behalf of the Technical Instruction Committee. Mr. Wilson said Sir John Brunner was not only a power and a help in their local affair!, but he was an element in the general educational policy of the nation. He was one of the men in the front rank of the great army of educationists who were battling for the advance. meat of humanity, and the thought they ought not to forget the fact that their object was to improve the quality of the young life of the nation, and to bring it to a higher citizennhip and a wiser manhood. Mr. Wilson, in the name of the Technical Instruction Committee, asked Sir John to accept an enlarged phetos graph of himself. [The photograph wail at this point un- veiled by Mr. Wilson amid loud applause.] Mr. Wilson continuing said they made the presentation as a token of the sympathetic regard they entertaiued towards him and his recognition of the wonderful work be had done for the people of Runcorn. (Hear, hear.) They sincerely hoped that the original would be with them for many years—(hear, hear)—to aid in any good work to which be had put his hand and his heart. (Loud applause). Sir John Brunner, who was received with applause, said they had that night paid to him the greatest com- pliment, he theught, that any set of MAR could pay to , one of their fellows. In asking him to dine with them and in presenting to him a portrait, they had adopted a form which was invariably looked upon as the highest honour that could be paid to an individual. It was a , very proud day for him that he should be thus honoured by men who ruled with such courage and wisdom, and who guided the destinies of that important town,which, amongst others, he had the honour to represent. Be was , proud of them. Mr. Taylor had referred to the many examples of the noble spirit of self-sacrifice that had been shown by them and by thoil constituents in the course of the erection of that building. It was indeed a noble response that came te the offer to which their Chairman had alluded, And it did his (Sir John's)heart good to know that many a inan,who could but ill spare the money, thought it well for his own sake and for his neighbour's sake to pinch himself for the purposes of the erection of that noble building. (Hear, hear.) He should, naturally, not say much about his part in the work. As they knew, many appeals were made to a member of Parliament,and he was very glad to see that some were protesting against the demands that were made upon them. He very frequently desired to join in the protest made by that noble army of martyrs and he thought they would sympathise with him when he said that to a very large proportion of the appeals that were made to him be had the courage to say No. This work, which had been eloquently described by Mr. Wilson. was work for the benefit of all, without distinc- tion of sex or creed. It war work to which his heart I went out, and it was work for which he was at all times ready to make the eacrifice that was called for. Neither of his friends on his right or left had alluded to the fact that Cheshire did honour to itself,and had for years done honour for itself,in putting itself apparently in the front I rank of all the counties in England and Wales in the efforts that it made for public instruction. (Hear, hear). Those who had studied his public utterances on the question that was filling their minds that night—the question of the drawing out of the qualities of the young amongst them—would have noticed that he had always steadily claimed for his countrymen that whatever work they took in hand they would do it as well and as thor- oughly as any nation under the sun. That was not an occasion for invidious comparisons between themselves and the various countries of Europe, but he should like for a moment to compare themselves with I themselves. Who would have imagined 10 years I ago that Runcorn would have been in possession of anything lik• that? Who would have imagined that the young people would have thronged into it as they were' doing ? Who would have imgined that, in the north of England at any rate—the south of England sometimes struck him as being inhabited by a rather different race, who were slower in their wits—that throughout the north of England, wherever these schools were put up, there the young people were thronging eagerly and anxiously to get in. (Hear,hear) The portrait was his and he was very loth to part with it. (Bear,hear) But a little bird had whispered to him that it would be a pleasing thing if he were to ask a friend of his to receive it at his hands as a gift to the people of Runcorn,and it was with a very fnll heart and a very proud mind that he asked Mr. Wiswall to receive it for Runcorn to he their property, as a memorial of a man who in his day tried to do his duty. (Loud applause) Mr. Wiswall said on behalf of the Technical Instruc- tion Committee and the ratepayers of Runcorn, he had very great pleasure Indeed—and he regarded it as an honour—to receive at Sir John's hands the photograph of himself. He could assure Sir John that they would value it much and place it in a prominent position in that building, to be looked upon by them as long as they lived, and by those who followed them. (Applause.) The Chairman proposed "the town and trade of Run- corn." fie coupled with it the name of a gentleman who had taken ,he deepest interest in the welfare of the town as far as its trade was concerned, and who had gone out of his way, not only to retain, but to increase the trade of the town. Be referred to Mr. Fred Norman. (Hear,hear.) Mr. Norman responded. Is a genuine Runcorn redtail, with the bump ot ! ,^al patriotism strongly developed in bum, he might be pardoned for suggesting or for rather emphasizing what Mr. Taylor had said, that this was after all the most important ts.ast of the evening. Of the good old town of Runcorn be should content himself with saying that she possessed historical tradi- tions that went far back into antiquity mad warranted her taking her place among the best municipal blue blood of the country. They were essentially a town of tradesmen, and the sooner they faced the fact the better it would be for the prosperty of their town, their citiz..nalaip and their in- stitutions. He (Mr. Norman) hoped, he need hardly. say, that he had never despaired, and never thought of

With 28 feet of water at their foreshore there was not the shadow of a doubt abouttitthat for many induaries there was no place better adapted tor them. Let them foster their trades and industries, cud, if they could,get a nuealser of capitalists to coma among them. (Applause.) The Warrington team was again badly drawn in the first round of the Northern Union Cup Ties,their first—and as it proved final—task being to meet Wakefield Trinity at Wakefield. Both teams have good records in cup-ties, the Trinity especially, and their very similar record to that of W arrington in League matches,made the probabilities all in favour of a close etruggle.Of the 300 spectators who accom- panied Warrington into Yorkshire few had any real belief that anything but defeat was in store for them, and yet there were fewer still withoat hope that perhaps luck would be on their side for once. The weather was of the best description for the trip and Wakefield was reached in good time. Warrington appeared as selected while the only al- teration in the Trinity team was the substitution of Bruales for Appleyard in the front rank. div.head: WILD BIRDS PROTECTION ACTS.
div.p: WILD BIRDS PROTECTION ACTS.

Under the Wild Birds Protection Acts, the Che- shire County Council gives notice that the taking or killing of wild birds is prohibited in the county of Chester from March 1 to August 12. All right- thinking people will commend the ruling of the Act, which prevents the extermination of our feathered songsters by that branch of pleasure- seekers carrying a shot-gun,and labelled sportsmen. The wild tirds are of no use dead, while alive they enhance the charms of Nature, and particularly in rural Cheshire, to a very large extent. This is all the argument rtquired for the justification of an order prohibiting their ruthless destruction. In another column we publish particulars of the order and the parishes it effects, hut the penalties of its infringement are vaguely, but none the less deter- rently, referred to only as those "mentioned in the said Acts."

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOHN RYLANDs, J.P.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOHN RYLANDs, J.P.
BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH.

I Warrington has lost another old and distin- guished townsman by the death of Mr. John Itylands, J.P., of the Grange, Thelwall, who expired at his Llandudno residence, Bryn Maelgwyn House Llanrhos, at half-past seven on Thursday last week. We need hardly,state with what deep regret news of his somewhat sudden demise was received in War- rin ton. It was sudden in the light of public ignor- ance of his precarious condition, though not unex- pected as he has been in delicate and failing health for years. The deceased gentleman went to Llan- dudno some months ago, where every care of his enfeebled frame was taken by his relatives and Dr. Craig. About a week ago,however,he caught cold and being powerless to throw it off, death supervened as stated above. Mr. Rylands was in his 85th year, and for more than half a century he has been inti- mately associated by business, political, and muni- cipal ties, with the town of Warrington. During his long career most of the public offices have been hatiourably filled by him,and naturally the associa- tions and friends made in such a lifetime are great in number. Regret at his death is there- fore exceedingly widespread. It is somewhat pathetic to reflect that the gallantry of a local constable last year in saving Mr, Rylands from a fatal accident has only prolonged his existence,a few months. The occasion will be rem embered by most people. Mr. Rylands had the, misfortune to be knocked down by a trap in Sankey-street, and would have been run over but for the promptness of a constable in seizing the wheel of the vehicle and forcibly diverting it from Mr. Rylands' pros- trate form. A sketch of his career is given below. It is almost needless to say that Mr. Rylands and his family have been long and intimately con- nected with Warrington and its immediate locality. The family to which he belonged was descended from an old stock of yeomen who had been settled in South West Lancashire for several generations. His father was t late Mr. John Rylands,of Be wsey House, Warringtn, and his mother was a daughter of the late Rev. James Glazebrook, vicar of Belton, Leicestershire. His father, Mr. John Rylands, was the celebrated juryman, who at the Lancaster Assizes, had stubbornly refused to join with the eleven other jurymen in bringing in a verdict of guilty in the trial for libel in which the father of Mr. Taylor, of the" Manchester Guardian," was the defendant, and who so impressed his colleagues, by his firmness and the cogency of his reasoning, as to I bring them all round to his opinions, or, at any rate, to agree to an acqeittal. Mr. John Rylands was born in Warrington in 1813, and was educated at the Boteler Grammar School, Warrington, of which the Rev. Thomas Vera Bayne, B.C.L. was at that time headmastee. Leaving school, the claims of business occupied his attention, and he has been closely connected with the firm of Rylands throughout his business career. Despite business cares Mr. Rylands found time to give attention to public affairs. elle took his share in procuring the incorporation of he Borough in 1847, and when that effort succeeded and the time came to elect the first town council in 1848, he was elected one of the early members. The town was divided into five wards, viz.: North East, North West, South East, South West,and Latchford. The last named ward r Aurned three members whilst the other wards each returned six. Mr. John Rylands was one of the successful candidates for the North East Ward, he being then known as Mr. John Rylands junit may be stated as a matter of iu- terest that Mr.Rylande was the lastbf the surviving gentlemen who composed Warrington's first Town Council. Mr. Rylands, it will be seen, has been an eye witness of the progress of the borough since its incorporation down to the present time, We brother Mr. Peter Rylands was chief magistrate of the borough in 1852-4,and another brother— Mr,Thomas Glazebrook Rylands—in 1858 9 served the town in a similar capacity. Mr. John Rylands; however, never occupied the position and his connection with the Council was not of very long duration. In the year 1861 he was appointed one of the borough auditors, a position which he filled with creslit and advantage to the town. He also rendered excellent service as chairman of the Warrington Assessment Committee, and served long in the difficult post of chairman of the Income Tax Commissioners in the borough. Mr.Rylands was one of the oldest of the borough magistrates, having been appointed in the year 1867 by the Crown. .lle was appointed a jus- tice of the peace for the county paler me of Lancas- ter on the sth August,lB6l ; and though his attend- ances on the bench during recent years have been few,owing to the state of his health and his numer- ous engagements, there was a time when he set a worthy example for regularity and punctuality. As a leading member of the Warrington Musical Society, and for many years its president, Mr. Itylands has done much to promote the love and practice of musical art in the town. He was an accomplished musician himself, and he took a great interest in the welfare of the Musical Society which in the course of ite chequered history has struggled with some success to create a love for high-class music. Mr. Ryland& was also a devotee of pictorial art, and at the time when the Warrington School of Art was under private management, gr. Rylands was chairman of the committee. The school owes much to his liberal and tastefel support. Another institution in which Mr. John Rylands took ass active and deep interest was the Warrington Infir- mary and Dispensary, of which he had long been life governor. - - -

Politically,he was an ardent and steadfast Liberal.and took an active interest in the elections of 1858 and 1874 when his brother,the late Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., was candidate. He has always been associated and closely identified with everything affecting the interests of the Liberal Party in the Borough, and the Lancashire and Cheshire County Divisions. Up to the time of his death Mr. Rylands was presiderr: of the Liberal Assn cia tioo, and it is rather a melancholy coincidence that only last Friday evening,at the meeting of the ex- ecutive of the Association he was re-elected for another , year. Latterly be has been physically unable to take any active participation in the affairs of the party, but for a long period during which he has filled thie office, he was a prominent speaker at and chairman of many important political meetings. That Mr. Rylands, like hiS eminent brother, the late Mr. Peter Rylands. M.P., took a keen interest in everything going on in the political world,wat evident to those who knew him and enjoyed his friendship: and while he was fair te his opponents,and treated them with the greatest possible courtesy and respect, he was ever read‘ to up- hold and defend his own convictions, and gives terser, for the faith that was in him. His descriptions of the y you,i 4 state of things which existed before Man meta now prominent in the politiral life of the borou :h were born were most entertaining, for, like the 14te Mr. McMinnies, he yossessed an almost inexhaustiole fund of anecdote. Everywhere his genial presence' lrs sound in good see, and his sympathy, with all that is kindly, enlightened, and progressive, made Mr. Ryla.„i, wel- come. As a business man Mr. Rylands had a busy life, and may be said to have been very successful. In addition to his long connection with the Arm which tears his name he was also closely associated with °thee business concerns, and wag:at the head of at least four compaMes. He was chairman of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited, chairman of Rylands Bros., Limited. Church-street, chairman of Mackie and Co., Limited, and chairman of Messrs. William Rey- nolds and Company. tanners, Mersey-street. Blesses. Rylands works were established by the father of the present proprietors amongst the earliest years of the century, and some considerable time ago they were formed into a limited comp tny under the Limited Liability Companies' Act. This was the first wirr-drawiog mill established in Warrington, and as may not unnaturally be supposed, great alterations and improvements in the wire manufacture have been in- troduced since it was opened. All of these which were of value were speedily adopted, and the establishment has been able to keep pace with the increasing require- ments of the trade. Some idea may be formed of the demands made upon the resources of the establishment when it is borne in remembrance that at the time it was started wire rope making was a thing undreamed of, wire fencing had not been introduced, and wire netting made by machinery had no existence. Now the manufacture of all these different descriptions of wire workingsmod many othere,is extensively carried on in the works under consideration. Several other wire works have sprung up in the town since that of the original Rylands was commenced. Wire-drawing, howe ever,although an important,and indeed,a leading featur of the industry carried on. here, is not by any means till only branch of manufacture for which the establishinen is famouq. In point of fact, almost every kind of pre paration to which wire is applicable is here carried on in the mostcomplete and Perfect manner The very latest improvements and inventions ar- brought to bear upon all the processes, and Messrs. Ry lands' works might well stand as a complete embodi ment of all that is known and practised in wire. working in the present day. The output of this singularly interest- ing end typical establishment is something enormous, and it is as remarkable for variety as it is for magni- tude. It embraces everything that is made of wire,

from a huge steel hawser to a picture cord, or from a yard of wire netting to a mile of barbed fencing. Of wire netting this company are the largest producers in the world. , With reference to Mr. Rylands' connection with the I Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, it may be stated that the Bewsey works of the Company— ' which were opened some 10 years after the Dallam forge was founded—were established in Bewsey-road, by a cAmpany consisting of Messrs. Rylamis Brothers, Mr. H. BlEckley and others. They were established for the manufacture of wire rode for the purpose of wire making and at first employed about 50 men and boys. With the increase of business at both the Bewsey and Hallam works the extensions made the land dividing the two less and less until at last the limit was reached, and the works adjoined each other. Before this occurred, how- ever, the amalgamation of the two works took place under the name of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company. It is to such men As Mr. John Rylands that Warrington holds its present position in the com- mercial world,whose personal exertions have done much for the development and present prosperity cot the town. Mr. Rylands was twice married. His second wife, and two sons and four daughters survive his loss. Mr. Edward and Mr. John Rylands are the two eons, and of the four daughters two are married—Mrs. John Bleckly, and Mrs. W. Reynolds.

div.head: LAT& MR. JOHN RYLANDS, J.P.
div.p: THE LAT& MR. JOHN RYLANDS, J.P.
POLICE COURT REFERENCES.

Allusion was made to the death of Mr. John Ryland, J.P., after the ordinary business at the Warrington Police Court on Monday. Mr. F. MONKS, C.C., (chairman), said, before they went ha should like to make some reference to the death of Mr. John Ryland, an old magistrate of the Borough. Although he bad not sat in that court as often as he used to do, he (Mr. Monks) voiced the feeling of the Bench when he expressed their regret at Mr. Rylands' death at the ripe age of 4 years. Mr. Tnomas BIacEALL said be should like to say that he remembered Mr. Rylands nearly all his life—half a century, and a more kindly man, or one who had made more friends and fewer enemies never lived in Warring- ton.

Alderman T. SUTTON said he had known Mr. Rylands as long, perhaps, as anybody in Warrington. In his youth he went to the Sunday School which Mr. RViands and his brothers and father kept in Flag-lane. And he must say that he derived a goo I deal of benefit from the instruction and education he got there. The loss of suck a man as Mr. Rylands would be a source of regret to everybody in the town. Alderman Hammon said he thought they were in ac- cord with the observation of the Chairman that Mr. John Rylands was certainly a very estimable character. He had the faculty of discharging a disagreeable duty in the most agreeable manner possible, and in such a way as not to jar upon the feelings of those whom he had sometimes to punish. He believed a more kindly disposition than Mr. Rylands' they could hardly love to lind,and it was a source of unalloyed regret that he had been taken away so suddenly, although he had lived to a ripe old age,beyond the limits assigned to man to live. He would be a very great loss.

div.head: 'ME TOWN COUNCIL AND MR. RYLANDS.
div.p: 'ME TOWN COUNCIL AND MR. RYLANDS.
At the meeting of the Town Couneil on Tuesday night the death of Par.Rylanda was refersed to. _. _

The MAYOR saidhe was sorry to have to report to them the death ef their well-known and respected townsman. Mr. John Rylands,at the advanced age of 83 years. Mr Rylands was the last surviving member of the first Town Council, elected more than 50 years ago, and his death had severed the last connecting link with the early history of municipal life in the borough. He had known Mr. Hylands himself from boyhood, and he had always held him in the highest esteem, as one of the most up- right and honourable men that ever he came in contact with. He begged to move :—"That this Council receives with deep regret the announcement of the death of Mr. John Ryland', formerly a member of this Council, and desires to express Re sincere sympathy with the family in their bereavement." Alderman Surrole said that as one of the oldest mem- bers of the Council be thought he ought to second that reaolution.He could quite corroborate all that the Mayor had said, and everyone who knew Mr. Rylands must know that he took a very active interest in everything connected with the affairs of the town,especially in mat- ters of education. It was no doubt owing to his energies 1 and perseverance,and his action along with others,that Warrington was in as good a condition as it was at the I present time—(bear, hear)—and that the trade of the , town and its general prosperity had increased to the ex- tent it had. (Hear,hear) Councillor H. ROBERTS said Mr. Rylands served the town faithfully and well for a long period, and was one of those man whose business enterprise, capacity and sagacity had done a great deal to make Warrington the town it was to-day. The chief regret was that the old generation of Warringtonians was now almost extinct. They had a groat deal of benefit from their advice and assistance in the past, and their example was a fitting one for them to follow in the future. The resolution was then carried.

div.head: PARR HALL CONCERTS.
div.p: THE PARR HALL CONCERTS.

The last of this season's Saturday popular con- certs given iu the Parr Hall a week ago was in every way a success. An admirable array of t -dent had been secured and one and all of these artistes acquitted themselves in a really creditable way The concert-loving public too, rallied in g;, )dly numbers, tilling every part of the hall and display- ing throughout the evening considerable enthusiasm in regard to many items in the programme. Mies Marie Burnett,Miss May Wayman, Madame Burelli. Miss Kate Beesley,and Mr. Arthur Weber,all of whom have before made their appearance at these concerts displayed their undoubted capabilities in such style as to secure the heartiest applause and the most iv • sistent encores and thus elicited the Mrongest testi-

mony to their popularity. Miss Mona r.L.;lare the danseuse, has also, we believe. alrAdy made her debut in Warrington eiqier alone or in company with some sisters similarly devoted to the fascinations of the light fantastic toe, and the unconscionable manner in wnich some portions of the audience clamoured for a third appearance in succession in what must be a fatiguing task almost led to some uproar. However more reasonable feel- ings at length prevailed and the due performance of the programme was resumed. The farcical sketches in which Miss Sybil Awdry and Mr. W. R. Duncan were associated were comparatively a new feature at these concerts and the really clever way in which these, we believe, original items were acted made them the most enjoyable of the evening and the evidence of the audience's appreciation was as well deserved as it must have been gratifying to the "Society entertainers" concerned. Miss Sophie Roberts played the piauo accompanimew.s on this occasion, as on many previous ones,with the best of taste.

!PEAR. N Et/SE,

_ When the afternoons are warm enough to dis- pense with wraps, coats of fanciful style will appear, and these will usually be made in bodice form, and require neither bodice nor blouse beneath. Many of the new models shown in Paris for early spring wear are of coat fashion, With short, tight basques, and arc almost invari- ably worn with a fancy belt. A very effective model coat is of Royal blue velvet, with folded revers, faced with biscuit-coloured moire, edged blue gimp, and vest of India muslin, with jabot of antique lace, and high, stiff collar. The skirt is of blue matelasse material, mounted on shot silk, and finished with pinked-out frills inside the edge. This is a very effective toilette in grey, the coat of grey ribbed velvet, with yellow revers, and vests of cream muslin and antique lace, and the jewelled belt with opaz and turquoise.

worn with this gown is a made mcsU, with crown of pale colour, sewn sequins, and folds of velvet rising on the left side with a cluster of ostrich plumes, and underneath the folds at the side big rosettes, mixed with the lighter colour On the right is a graceful home toilette of helio- trope vigogne in the new reddish tint, and this is made with a yoke-plastron of beige guipure over gleaming white satin, and the trimming of fancy braid is carried over the guipure yoke in brace fashion.

a toilette in light-coloured cloth, with dark fur, and narrow crystal and sequin passementerie looks well. The jacket yoke is outlined with a shaped berthe arrangement, kept stiff, and the tucks be- low the yoke are varied by a double frill of wavy chiffon. The sleeve is quite close-fitting and tucked above the elbow, and then trimmed with fur and passementerie to simulate a separate pouff.

This gown is cat in princess° form, wide exten• lions falling out on either side of the centre back pieces, these arranged in pleats on the inside. The back portions should be lined throughout with thin horsehair cloth. The front is arranged with sides lapping over the centre gore to simulate a long coat shape, and this style is especially effective, and allows the gown to 14vten in front, but slightly to the left side.

Guipure over satin is very smart, and if the piece guipure is employed, this can be finished at revers and basque with a narrow guipure insertion, thus giving the effect of a shaped vest. The coat is cut in the new cut-away fashion, and is very becoming to a flat or slight figure. The coat could also be copied in cloth to accompany a skirt, and arranged with a vest of white or light-coloured cloth, and habit-front of cambric worn with a tie.

A coat for early spring wear appropriate for morning wear should be supplemented by 61. fur, and a muff en suite, or on warm days with simply a jabot of lace. The skirt and coat are of cloth, with three-quarter inch braid. The coat is lined with coloured silk, and a silk blouse completes the toilette.

Between-season gowns must, I am afraid, be regarded as luxuries rather than necessities ; nevertheless, it may not be amiss to describe two or three of the newest models which may be safely regarded as examples of what will be worn. One of the most important features in the new dresses is the cut of the skirt, which, to be in accordance with the latest dictum of fashion, must be very close-fitting at the top, but wide and well-shaped at the hem, although quite devoid of anything in the way of stiffening, so that it hangs in heavy, decidedly inconvenient folds round the feet. 1¢ some models the requisite wideness of the lower half of the skirt is achieved by adding a kind of shaped flounce at the level of the knees, but the i majority are cut n one. Trimmings are not universal by any means, yet many smart skirts are adorned with scanty cross- out flounces of various widths, bands of braiding or applique, or have their seams accentuated, with some kind of garniture. Close-set perpendicular tacks are often seen on the hips or even extending right round the top of the skirt, and in not a few eases these tiny pleats are further ornamented with rows of very small gold or silver buttons. Your loving Jima.

div.p: 'OMEN'S CEIAT.

Several grey horse l from the Royal stud, and the Queen's favourite donkev,which with the carriage have been despatched to Cimiez, there to await the arrival of the court, are being exercised daily, in order to be- come familiarised with the roads they will have to traverse. The royal carriages intended for the use of her Majesty's excursions from Cirni( z include a landau and a sociable,also the donk-y chaise in which the Sovereign will take her morning drive within the grc,unds of the hotel, or those of the adjacent Villa Liserb. The whole expenses ot the Continental trip are under- stood to represent something like £1,200. The Queetex party and suite comprise together something like seventy persons, and the visit entails an immense amou:lt of preparation, as it is one of her Majesty's rules that her own rooms shall be made as nearly as possible like her private apartments at Windsor, much ot her own furni- ture, many knicknacks, photographs, and personal trifles for the writing table, &c., being taken from her own palaces. One very interesting feature of Cimiez is a Breton farm, and yet another, the Monastery of the Reeellets, originally founded in N;CP, but destroyed by Barbarossa in 1543, alter which the monks bcught the site of the present edifice from the Abbot of St,Pons.

With the exception of the large equestrian picture nf the Prince of Wales, and the Duke of Connauzht, rio decision has yet been arrived at, concerning the dispesi- ton of the Diamond Jubilee gif,s. It is anticipated however, that instruetions on this peint will he given by Her Majesty shortly. The picture mentiened has now been placed permanently in a mural panel created for it by the removal of three mirrors from the west wall of the State Dining Room in Windsor Castle. Alms in the suite of rooms, comprising the East ['err ice, the dining room hitherto possessed no pietorial relief upon its walls, and the result of the change is distinctly pleasing. Speaking of Windsor, among the royal palaces of Europe, the Castle lays claim, and justly, to the first place. Some, like the old fortress of the Popes on the rocky Cliffs by the Rhino may he more perfect in archi- tecture, others like Heidelherg, may surpass it in beauty !of site, some again, like the Escurial, ma l's larger, but in none are size, beauty, and grandeur, so united, as in the first and oldest of our Royal residences. The attempt to assassinate King George, has added still further to the troubles which have fallen of late upon the Greek Royal Family. Happily the attack was not a successful one, still, neither Queen Olga, or any member of the %file's family, can know much peace of mind for some considerable time to come. roe Princess of Wales has suffered somewhat severely from the anxiety she has experienced since the news of the attempt on her favourite brother's life reached this country. . .

- I Although the mother of seven children, and in every I sense a true help-meet to her husband, Queen Olga hss always taken an active part in the found tion and organisatien of Greek charities. Ole of the most ad- mirable hospitala in the world is at Athens, and was started by the Queen, and a few of her ladies same ten years back. See ii actively connected with this institu- tion and once or twice a week visits the kitehens and wards, to see that all is well managed in each depart- ment. Queen Olga is a great favourite with her husband's nephews and nieces, the Duke of York in par- ticular being fondly attached to his aunt. To her has been addressed one of the first telegram,' Announcing the birth of each of Ms Royal Hi mess's children. 'The ceseatien as to whether early rising conduces to lengevity has lately been raised in one of the Landon papers,and after much consideration has been answered in the affirmative. Most persons who have lived to be old have been good sleepers, bet this does not mean that they have been long sleepers. A good sleeper is one who sleeps well. Fie may sleep vita enough in six or seven hours to answer all his need, and it would be folly for him to be in bed three or four hours more. As a Mit>, long lived persons have been early risers because they have been good sleepers. Bc " good sleep " is me ,nt sleep that is sweet acid sound; without dreaming. Those who love to rise early, generally have street; wills, and good health to begin with. Late risers are often inv 'lids Cr persons of had habits; idlers, who are never free from other vices besides MI ryes. The Queen still adheres to the habits of her youth, in the matter of early rising, and is awakened soon after seven in the morning. Tier Majesty then takes a cop of eocoa and some biscuits, and at eight she rises. The Princess of Wales, it. true now allows herself an extra hour in the morning, hut ur"til her children were criite grown up Her Royal Highness made it a rule to be up and ready for the day's duties at nine o'clock. The Harris tweeds which appear this season in many fascinating and delicate colors, are simply ideal fabrics for cycling, and for early spring walking gowns. They have only one fault—they positively retuse to wear out. There have been too, some particularly deliehtfol tartan fabrics placed upon the marker of late,and in Paris these have met with a most enthusiastic reception. French• women have ever a great affection for a pleiri fabric, no matter how wildly impossible from the Scotch paint of View, the combination Of colors may chance ta he. Many of the new skirts are somewhat heavy, the full- nese near the hem having a swathing feeling, which J. rather trying until one becomes accustomed to it. And the majority will only prove becoming to those who are thoroughly well proportioned. Even very slender women will not regard the newest skirts with fever, as they do not hang well over pronounced anatomical de- velopments. Really, at the moment, a fine figure seems to be of alters value to a member of our MPS than a pretty face. There are of course some fortunate Senn"n • who possess both—the Princess of Walee,Lady Flaetings, Lady Tweedrneuth, Georgina Lady Dadley,fOr instance, --hut they are few and far, between. It is a well-known fact that although wernan are free qeently witty they are seldom humoreus. 'This Statn of 1 affairs is co be regretted, as it is certain that wit makes more enemies than friends r .er a woman unless she is very careful in her utterances. A refined and delicate humanr, on the other hand, is especially charming. A woman who will recount her worries and difficulties and bear them in a humouroim and pleasant faehien is stirs ,to be much beloved by her surroundings. To make mountains out of molehills, and a burden of a grass- hopper 'me still a filling of the female mind, whose life is lees ye ried end wheee horizen of neceeeity, lees dis- ' tart than are those of mankind. A wider range of Pima, a breeder mind, and larger sympathies are all needed fee a tree and eurneerous Appreciation of email events, and the balancing of the daily elements of life. It is semewhat difficult to keep abreast with all the modern theories af health and di: t,vet at the risk of be- ing sometimes made a little uncemfortahle it is as well to knew what is being said by exeerts upon these im- portant subjects. The latest diecover*,trade by an em- inent Frenchman is, that soup is the canoe of almost all the misfortunes of dyspeptic patients ? There is, he soundly declAres,hardly any neurishment in it,moreovere it prevents one from extraeting any from the solid foods taken after it,since it hinders their digestion. It Rim injures the teeth. Se another popular article of diet has fallen under the ban. .

"I had given myself up. Thinking my work in this world was at an end, I bad begun to prepare tor the next. The knowledge that I was consumptive was a terrible blow."
So spoke Mr. F. Joyce, of 5, Brown's Buildings, Wesi rottergate-street, Norwich.

I Up to August, 1998, he bad enjoyed fairly good health, but then a change came. Be felt sick and languid, un- able to move about, and be lost interest in the ordinary affairs of life. Every morning he raised phlegm which was streaked with blood ; and he lost over a stone in weight. His breathing, too, was short and painful. Mr. Joyce's apprehension was increased by the fact that his father had died cf consumption. He went to two doctore, but withcut benefit. Then one morn- me, to ire his own words. the Norwich Eastern Daily Press I read a case of a consumptive young man, who bad beau spitt- ing up blood and having nights sweats, who was restored to health and strength by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. I procured a box of these Pills myself, and followed the directions, with the result that after three toxes I felt as well as I ever did in my life' Mr. Joyce now submitted him- self, for examination at the Nor- folk and Norwich Hospital. The doctors of that great institution declared him to be in a sound state of health, and refused to supply him with any medicine. " The change," said Mr. Joyce, " was due entirely to Dr. Williams Pink Pills."

Mr. Joyce has advised several ailing friends to try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. A man named Haynes, of Bull Close, Norwich. whose brother died of consumption, recently feeling unwell, consulted a medical man who told him his right lung was effected. He finally resorted Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, which made him a new man. Another friend of Joyce's was recently discharged fr m the Navy, on the ground that he was in a.consumption. He took a few boxes of Dr. Williams' Pink Pillf, and has just passed the medical examination to which persons who wish to enter the service of the railway companies are subject.

RUNCORN VERSUS ULVERSTON.

In the draw for the -first round- in the above competition, the Cestrians had to make the long journey to Ulverston,on Saturday. In view of the long distance, the Runcorn Club ap- proached the Mverston Club to play the match at Run- corn, but they declined the offer,thinking that they had a good chance to win in view of the performances o the Runcornians since Christmas. Both teams had bee in training, and inducements had been made to th home team by offering them a bonus if they won. Run corn had done their training at night, the Drill Hal having been kindly placed at their disposal by Colonel Ash'on. Runcorn were unable to play their strong- est team, West, Langley, and Darlington being unable to make the journey. This materially altered the composition of the team originally chosen, Robin- son having to go from half back to the centre position, Jolley filling the vacancy, and Warder taking up his old position in the three-quarter line after several weeks' absence. Ulverston were fully repre- sented. The following was the composition of the teams :-171yerston : Afurphy,back; R. Rebinson,Hine, Platt, and Hall, three-quarter backs ; McDonald and Newby, half backs ; Elliott, Stainton, Jackson, Turner, Whittle,Robinson. Duke, and Porter,forwards. Runcorn: S. florrehton,heek ; T. Warder,J. Butterworth,G, Robin- son,and G. Woods,three-quarter backs ; J. Faulkner and J. Jolley,balf hacks ; S. Walker. G. Moores, H. Farmer, W. Lightfoot, F. Gayter.S. Johnson, W. Bettley, and T. Antrobus,forwards. Referee, R. Ashton (Werneth). A strong breeze was blowing from goal to goal when Far- mer started for Runcorn, who had lost the toes and had to fags the sun and wind. The opening stages saw the hems team quickly en the aggressive, and aided by the wind they had much the hest of matters, and quickly scored several minors. The first movement which thlratened danger was initiated by McDonald • and R. Robinson WAS given a chance,but the passing movement was much too slow. Houghton defended his charge with groat Judgment, and never attempted to kick in face of the strong wind, but adopted the rushing tactics. The whole of the Runcorn backs Were playing a grand deign- give game and the Efiverston passing was quickly nipped I tithe bud. Gradually, Runcorn forced their way to their opponents' quarters, and ROM pretty passing was witnessed, Jolley and Faulkner starting several move- ments which caused the lllveratonians to have an anxious time of it. Hall by judicious kicking gave re- lief, but it was soon evident that Runcorn bad the mem- cure of their opponents, they rarely failing to make headway when the ball became loose. After several minors had been conceder,chiefly by long kioking.Joiley broke away, and another round of passing saw Divers- ton defending. Hine intercepted when a score seemed certain, and play was once more located near the Roncorn lines. From the following scrimmage, passing between Faulkner, Robinson and Warder saw the latter in possession, and racing away from the half-way line, he eluded his opponents cleverly, and scored a try, Jolley failing at goal. Stimu- lated by this success the Cestrians fairly warmed to their work, and although aided by the elements, Tilverston never really looked dangerous. However, they were re- warded just before the interval, as the Runcornians being a little too previous, the :ball was placed for Platte, who kicked a goal from near the centre of the field. This success wag hailed with delight by the home partizses, but nothing further was scored to the interval when the position *al Runcorn, one try (three points) ; Ulverstrn. one toal (,wo points). Tio second portio soon saw Runcorn on the attack, and after smart pas ing Botterworth sent the ball sailing over the bar. The restart brought no relief for the home team. The Runcorn forwards had possession from nearly every pack,with the consequence that Faulkner and Jolley got their hacks in working order,and the result was that Butterworth ran in a couple of tries,both of which were unconverted. The game was very one-sided, and nevee once did lllverston reach the half way. Robinson was the next to add to the score by way of a dropped veal. The passing of the whole of the Runcorn backs was al- most faultless, and only for the high wind the seers ould have been much larger,as many movements were spoiled by the wind carrying the hail forward. It was evidently Butterworth' "day out," for before the finish he put on a couple more tries which brought his share for the afternoon up to one drooped goal and four tries. Ulverston defended atubbornly,but the all round combin- ation of the visitor; elmpletely out-classed them, the final scare being—lloncorn,2 goals, five tries (ig points); Ulverton, one goal (two points).

Mini violet Warren, schoolmistie.ss, living yrith her uncle and aunt, Mr. and Mre. Humberstone, at Wrestling - worth, Bedfordshire, is a bright, higlhy.educ'ated lady, in perfect health, but has bad a narrow escape from death by consumption. She said : " I had a splendid doctor to attend Me for three years, but grew gradually worse. For months I could not go downstairs. At last the doctor despaired. He said I vras in a consumption, and told my relatives I could net live long. .Sliiv sister was sent for from Northumberland, to see for the last time. But I was persuaded to try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. For the first few days I did not seem to make much progress, but within a week my appetite returned I sent for a mut- ton chop, a thing I had not been able to eat for a very long time. div.head: WIDNES v. LITERSEDGE.
div.p: WIDNES v. LITERSEDGE.

Widnes being drawn against Liversedge, the wooden spoonists of the Yorkshire section in the first round of the cup dee, the fifteen met at Widnes on Saturday in fine,though boisterous, weather. The start was delayed half an hour owing to the late arrival of the visitors. Liversedge started, and after a few exchanges at the centre, in which Widnes claimed the advantage,Brennan , and Rispan were early prominent with a smart passing ' movement, which Wallace only checked on the line. Rispan dropped without effect, and, the home backs working well upon the left wing, Brannan gave a pass to Nevitt, who scored, Batey failing with the kick. A round of wearisome scrummag,icg took place in the visi- tors' 25, and after Rispan had given Brennan a bad pass when an opportunity of scoring presented itself Batey kicked a penalty goll for Widnes. Liversedge by spas- modic play at length got into the Widnes half, and a good kick by Rispan was well returned by Wallace. A grand round of passing shared in by all the Widnes backs ended in Peters scoring at the corner, Baty' e kick going a trifle wide. By the aid of a free kick Widnes got away to their opponents line,and after some fantastic play by the Widnes forwards Baty kicked enothar penalty goal, the ball striking the upright and rebound- ing through. Grace sprinted right across the field, and from an ensuing movement Douglas scored for Widnes, Baty again failing to add two points. The Widnes full back again kicked with no success from a penalty for obstruction, and then Heslop scored, no goal resulting. Widnes were now playing a man short,Harnpson having sprained his thigh. Half-time : Widnes 2 goals 4 tries, Liversedge nil. Widnes restarted and Liverevdge came down, and the hall was put in touch in the home quarter. Brennan, Nevitt, and Batey relieved,and Rispan,securing the ball, threw it to Brennan, who had a clear field, and gained a try. Batey placed a goal. Liversedge again foiced the home players back, and from a cenalty Wallace made a poor attempt at goal. Nevitt, Peters, and Murphy ran, and passed splendidly, and Liversedge had to defend their lines. The visitors eventually cleared to the home half, where a free kick p'aced them on the at- tack. Fine passing by Hunt, Rieman, and Nevitt, how- ever, again transferr, d play to the visitors' quarter,and Heslop rushed over, Batey placing a goal,Travie and one of the visitors were ordered off the fild Final score : —Widnes, four goals and six tries(26 points);Liversedge nil. BIRKINURAD WANDERTRS V. RUNCORN RECREATION.— The junior Runcornians visited MI henhead on Saturday, to try their strength against the Wanderers, and a large 'crowd assembled to visit the game, which was played in beautifully bright weather. Watson started against the wind, which was blowing strongly from the Bidston end. The three-quarters at once got off, and Watson was downed on a line,rnissing a c?rtain try by failing to pass. A drop at goal by ftigham went dead. The home backs mulled after a drop out ; but Holmes and Morgan came to the rescue with an able dribble, to which Wright replied by a long kick, which registered another minor. Then Heyespassed out grandly to Liversage, who put on a really rite run and scored cleverly, and Holmes made a splendid shot at gnal—just missing. The home team pressed after re-starting, and Jones kicked over the line. Watson's failure to pass lost several fine chances to his side. Play soon went to the other end, , Ingham at full-back being over run, and but for brit- I liant play by Murphy, the Rocs, were over. They pressed hard and forced a touch down. Dillon tried Co be too smart and was downed in proper style, the Recs. still keeping up the pressure, and the others playing a very poor game. There was no further score. Half-time : Birkenhead Wanderers I try, Runcorn Recs. nil, Run- corn restarted against the breeza, and the Wanderers, in suite of their bad play, were so helped by the wind that the attacked strongly, and had four minors in quick succession. At lsst, after many failures, Arthur Jones got ovi-r from A forward rush, and Watson landed a nice goal. Final result :--Birkenhead Wanderers 1 goal 5;1 tries (17 points). Runcorn Recreation nil.

WESTON V. Runners HOENETs.—Played at Runcorn. The Hornets won the toss and played against the wind. Pendlebury earteci, Hughes being tackled before return- ing. The Weston baoks tried hard to get through the Homers' defence, but were soon repulsed. hycestartql oassf my movement, but was soon driven bark. P- Wiliams shot at goal, but the ball went outside. Pendle- bury now scored' far out, Dunbavin falling at goal. The Weston forwards gave their backs plenty of chances to shins, but the finishing touch was wantihg. Half-tiree was reached without any further score, The Hornets re- started, a good return being made. Weston forwards still kept getting the best of the scrimmages, but the Hornets were the beet on the !none. A bit of misunder- standing by the Weston backs allowed the Hornets to dribble over, Hall failing to kick dead. Stringer kicked a goal from the restart. Exciting play now followed, P.

Williams, Pendiebary, Glynn, and Dunbavin tried hard to score, but the Hornet's defence was strong. The Hornets' forwards again got away, bat Molyneux was safe at back. 'rime w:is now reaelvd, thu Llmaets win- ning by 1 goal, 1 try to Weston 1 try.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOROUGH GYMNASIUM.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOROUGH GYMNASIUM.
SCHOOL CHILDREN'S DRILL COMPETITION.

The Gymnasium was inconveniently crowded on Monday evening on tl4e occasion of the school child- ren's drill competition. Great interest was taken in Lhe event, and the attendance was so large that many were unable to find seating accommodation. The competition is the outcome of the classes for school children which have been commenced this session at the Gymnasium, and judging by the suc- cess which attended it, it will probaby become an annual institution.

Councillor Tinnion presided, and amongst those also present were the Mayor(Alderman Wright),Mr. D, Jones (chairman of the Gymnasium Committee). Alderman Eutton,Councillor .Evans,the Rev. Father Po!den, Rev. F. Slater, Messrs. Gorse, Dimmelow, Vernon, and others. .

In opening the proceedings, Councillor Tinnion delivered a brief address. Ile referred to the work of the Gymnasium as being a vary useful and ne- cessaty one. He thought it was a great necessity that the child should be strengthened in its body by rational exercise,_ and thus better equipped for the battle of life. He was pleased to say that the committee of the Gymnasium had been greatly en- couraged by the assistance they had received from the managers of the schools in the town. (Hear, hear.) Seeing that the gymnasium was now an institution of the Corporation's it was the duty of the committee to make it of use to the public of the town, and he thought they were en- gaged in a very useful work. As an instance of the extended use to which the gymnasium was now being put, he might state that from September 6th, to Februazy 24th, the attendances of school chil- dren were 13,430 boys, and 13,003 girls. (Applause.) In addition 3174 attendances had been made at the ordinary classes of the institution, so that the total amounted to 29,607, or an average of 1345 per week, (applause.) He hoped that the institution would be -still further suecessful and that the people of Warrington would receive the benefit which was to be derived from it. He thought there would be many who would bless the day that the Gymnasium was taken over by the Corporation. (Applause.) Six schools entered the competition, and they were represented by teams of twelve boys and twelve girls. The boys exercised with dumbells and the girls with barbells. The exercises were the same for each school, and the medals which were awarded were for the best performances Mr. C. Lowe, of Manchester, was the judge, and his deci- sions gave general satisfaction. The six competing schools were : Trinity, St. Mary's (But termarket- at.), St. Alban's, St. James', St. Paul's, and Wycliffe. The boys' team of St. Alban's was placed at a dis- advantage owing to the absence of one of the boys selected which only entitled the team to a maxi' mum of 110 marks as against 120 for the other teams. The exercises were gone through to the accompaniment of the piano which was presided at by Miss Clayton. Taken as a whole the performances of the ehildien were exceptionally well done, and it was only by noting little techni- calities here and there that the judge was able to distinguish the beet teams. It was apparent that Mr. J. Kinsley, in his capacity of director of exer- cises had taken considerable pains in the training of the children. The contest sas entered into with great earnestness, and each school seemed deter- mined to excel. The audience were delighted with the performance, and showed their approval by re- peated applause. The winning teams were 1118 follows :—Boys: Ist, (silver medals), Wycliffe ; 2nd, (bronze medals),Trinity ; Girls: Ist (silver medals)' St. Alban's ; 2nd (bronze medals), St. Paul's. The following were the scores : School.

div.p: EXHIBITIGN OF lIYACINTHS AT
WARRINGTON.
COUNCILLOR JOHN CROSFIRLD'S GIFT.

It will probably be remembered that in October last gear,Couneillor John Crosfield, J.P., generously distributed gratis among the working-classes of the town,about 1,500 hyacinth bulbs,with a view of en- couraging a taste for horticulture. Each recipient received three varieties—a red, white and blue— and the conditions were that the plants were to be , grown either in pots or glasses in the recipients' 'dwellings, and it was announced that prizes would be given at a later period for the best blooms. The exhibition of these blooms took place on Saturday afternoon in the upper front room of the Warring- ton Gymnasium. There was an excellent display, aud it Was evident that the bulbs had received caret ul treatment at the hands of those woo received them. There were staged for exhibition 170 pots and 120 glasses, and as these were interspersed with foliage plants, kindly lent by tbe Corporation, the effect was very pleasing. In the course of the afternoon the show was visited by a great number of people, who seemed agreeably surprised at the excellence of the exhibits. SUN DAY OBSERVANCE. Sir,—Some few years ago the very interesting letters we have seen in your correspondence calumn during the the last few weeks could not have seen the light in a newspaper. It used to be thought that " sacred " sub- jects ought not to be discussed in secular papers ; why. I never could understand. What appertains to the pear Is and their welfare ought surely to be discussed by the people in the people's journals. First, we had " Ion;" and R. G. L. hammering away at Sunday observance; without in my opinion, touching the rock of the matter. For Sunday observance as a day apart for extra-religious observance there is not a tittle of scrip- tual warrant from Genesis to Revelations. 'De heathen sun-worshipping Emperor Constantine determined for his own convenienze to amalgamate the Christian seventh. day Sabbath with his own Dies Solis Sunday the"vener- able day of the Sun" as he called it. This change effected without Scriptural warranty is now continued in these latter days as a matter of conveinence. It matters little at what end of the week we get the much needed mental and bodily rest so long as we do get it. Constantine broke the law and we are content with the fragments.—Truly yours, IS-'S. (The correspondence on this subject is now closed—Ed

- FORTHCOMING ELECTION OF GUAR- DIANS AMD PARISH COUNCILLORS. The triennial election of Guardians and Rural District Councillors in the Warrington Union and Rural District will take place within the next few weeks, and no doubt considerable interest will be aroused. Already several names have been sug- gested as probable candidates,but of course nothing definite will be known until the nomination papers have been handed in. In Warrington two repre- sentatives of the Trades and Labour Council retire ' from the Board of Guardians,viz.: Mr. 'r. B. Malkin, and Mr. A. Lang, who represent Bewsev and St. John's wards respectively. Mr. Lang w:11 net seek re-election. The Trades Council have chosen Messrs. Malkin, Delaney, and Battersby as their candidates for nomination. The retiring Guardian 3 in War- rington are as follows :—Town Hall ward, Mr. A. J. Jolley ; Whitecross ward, Mrs. Clay; Bewsey ward. Thomp- son ; Latchford ward,Mr. A. Jolley. We understand that all the members, with the exception of Mr. Lang, and probably Mr. Shaw,alluded to, will seek re-election. The last day and hour for sending in nomination papers to the offices of the Returning Officer, Bewsey-street. is 12 o'clock noon on the 17th -March. The poll will take place on the 4th of April.
