THE NEW NURSING ORDER.- A SUPERINTENDENT NURSE TO BE APPOINTED.

The House Committee's minutes stared that the report of a conference betwe n the Chairman and Mr. H. Jen- ner Fust anent the new nursing order was surimitted, and after consideration thereof, it was recommended that a surwrintendent nurse, qoalified under that order be advertised tor at a salary of £45 per annum, with apartments, rations, and an allowance of £5 per annum in lieu of uniform,also that a nurse he obtained from the Nursing Association a", a salary of 225, rising to £27 103, at the end of the first vear,with the usual apartments.— Mr. A.J. Jolley moved the confirmation of the minutes. —The 11217. J. H. Riddette seconded, and expressed hi ereat pleasure that they were now taking a great steps forward, which would bring their Infirmary into line with the best managed institutions of the country.—Mr. Alfred Jolley said he was very sorry he was not present at the last meeting as vice-chairman of the committee, but he should certainly support the actien of the mem- bers. He quite agreed with the step which lad been taken.—The minutes were carried. THE INDUSTRIAL EXHIBITION.

The MASTER informed the Board that Mr. Hooper, thq manager of the forthcoming Industrial Exhibition at Parr Hali,had invited the inmates to attend. HA would peovide them with refreshments. The invitation was accepted.the selection of the inmates for the visit to rest with Mr. Ward. A VOTE OF SYMPATHY.

Mr. BiLmNon moved a vote of sympathy with Mr. S. Davies, a member of the Board, who, he stated, had sustained a severe !oat; by the death of his oldest daughter. Mr. Davies had filled all the prominent posi- tions in connection with the Board, but sickness in his family had recently prevented him from attending to his duties as a Poor Law Guardian with his accustomed regularity.—Mr. Thompson seconded the vote, and said he was sure all the members sympathised with Mr. Davies in his bereavement.—The Chairman also spoke in sympathetic terms, and the vote was unanimously earned.

THE USE OF CALF LYMPH FOR VACCINATION. Dr. Parreasms, in accordance with notice of motion given at the last meeting of the Board moved the folio w- ing resolution:—"That on and after the close of the present March half-year the question whether in any particular case, calf lymph should be used for public vaccination be determined by tho public vaccinator,and it be a recommendation that calf lymph be used for pub- lic vaccieation whenever it is requested by the parents, provided the public vaccinator himself feels that sueh use of calf lymph will meet with satisfactory results,and that for each case of successful public vaccination done with calf lymph the public vaccinator be paid the sum of sixpence in addition to the usual fee for such vaccina- tion." Dr. Patterson observed that if this plan were adopted it would take away a great deal of the ill-feeling which was at present felt with refermuce to compulsory vaccination. When children were vaccinated with calf lamph the parents might be sure that disease would not be communicated as was perhaps liable uader the system of arm to arm vaccination. The lymph was specially prepared,and was micrnsopically examined so as to preventlthe possibility of it being able to c en- snunicate diseaAe.—The Chairman said he somewhat sympathised with anti-vaccinators. They were aware that many cows suffered from tuberculosis, and it was possible that a calf,although it might not have develop.d that disease, might still be able to transmit it to others. He did not see where the advantage of calf lymph came li. If children were vaccinated at all it was quits as well to take the matter from a healthy child in prefer- ence to calf lymph. There was also another point which he believed was correct and that was that calf-lymph did not act as well on' child as through a human me- dium.—Mr.Billinee vconded the resnlution,and said the matter had been before the Newton Committee, and approved of.—The Rev. J. H. Riddette said the Newton Committee sanctioned the use of calf lymph but not the resolution before them. No thought the resolution as drawn up left a loop hole for the vaccination officer to refuse to vaccinate with calf lymph when requested to do so. fle would move an amendment that the words" provided the public vac- cinator himself feels that such use of calf lymph will meet with satisfactory results "be left eut.—Mr. A. J. Jolley said the resolution had been drawn up in accord- ance with the Local Government Board's communication on the subject.—Mr. Thompson seconded the amend. mint—Mr. Hibbert said several attempts bad been made to vaccinate him, but on every occasion it had never taken. (Laughter.)—The Aeslstant Clerk read the communications from the Local Government Board,and it was ultimately agreed that the reselution as it stood could no be altered.—Dr. Patterson's motion was there- fore Passed. THE INDUSTRIAL BOYS AND THE NAVY. The Rev. J. H. Rinowera said he would like to know whether ally opportunity was given to the boys at the Board'e Industrial school at Padeate, to go to sea. He thought such boys as they had in their institution were well fitted for the Nsvv.—The Chairman said at a recent conference on theeubject in Manchester,it was shown to them that it was almost impossible to get such boys into the Navy, as the restrictiene wer• 50 great, and the re- quirements in height, girth, etc., so exacting. The up- Shot of the conf-rence was a recommendation to send workhouse boys to training ships.—Mr. A. J. Jolley said the committee was endeavouring to get one of the boys at the Industrial School into the Navy. They had been rn..t with difficalties set up by relatives in the past, but he believed sum a le!islation on the subject Was to take place. (Hear, heer).—The enhiect then dropped. THE NEW INFIRMARY. The CLIME forwarded a letter to the Board referring to the !nen on the new Infirmary. stating that in a Sew days he hoped to be in the position of having £IO,OOO of the money to be advanced at the disposal of the coin- mittee.—Several members expressed aatisfacvion at the progress which the contractor was making in the build- ing of the institution. HABITUAL DRUNKARDS. A communiea'ion Wa. read askine the Board to mm- port a MPTIVIrjai to the 1,-)nal Government Board with reference to habitual dru )kerie, urging that on suffici- ent pr twine furnished of any person being an habi- tual drunkard, he or elle might he certificated for corenailaory detention in like manner as is now done under the sCvo'-al acts for the detention of lunatics on necessary Safeguards being provided to prevent abuse.— un the proposition of the Rev. J. H. Riddette, seconded by Mr. A. J. Jolley, it was decided to accede to the request. This concluded the husines•.

Shortly after nine o'clock on Friday morning, last a "riOU4 accident occurred at the works of the Castner• Kellner Alkali CO., Limited, 'Weston Point. It appears that Some seven or ,ight man were engaged whitewash- ing new ehip, and for this purpose they stood on a scaffild 25 feet from the Baer. RUGBY FOOTBALL. YE KUP-TYES.

So it's good-bye to th, eup,and in Vie first round too. Wakefield just Marlow • 4 get the verdict by five points to three, and for the fi: ime in their history Warring- ton received the knock- in the opening round of a eup.competitioa. Thou. • dl the :fiances seemed on the Wakefield aide, I think t eybody from Warrington had a sneaking belief that their ielected fifteen might, for once, catch tne smile of D Fortune ani emerge suc- cessful from the ordeal. F mcball generally, and cup-tie football in particular is IQ productive of surprises, that no Case can seem quite hapless, sod therefore the gallant band of 300 might be excused their optimis- tic feelings whed departing for Yorkshire. A. similar healthy belief in their own powers pervaded the minds of the players themselves, and It is sot too much to say that the defeat was a bigger disappointment to them thaa anyone else. Dame Fortune could not be coaxed, and though the gallant Warringtianians played like demons and deserved to win, they were compelled to bid goodbye to the trophy which Batley captured last season.

Contrary to expectations,the day arrived with bright sunshine and a drying breeze. The previous night rain was falling with a persistency which augured ill for a wall contested game on the following day. Everything was satisfactory at the euteet. A well-appointed special drew up punztually at 11-30 a-m in the Central Station and was soon filled by the excited followers of the club. The accommodation provided by the Cheshire Lines Committee was first-class in several respects. There were saloons galore, and a number of reserved " firsts " for dignified officials, and more or less ateolfied pressmen. It was a comfortable and expeditious jcw,-;1v to the cathedral town of Wakefield, which was reac‘-e 1 before I p-m. With an hour to spare there was time to get a "snack," and this peculiarly Lancashire subsititute for "a feed" was soon got outside of by those who felt the need of it.

The match was played in Santal Magna. Perhaps you did not know that, and thought it was played at Wake- field. Well ! it wasn't, but at Santa! Magna. It wasn't played here because of its being a cup-tie -but for the sole reason that Wakefield Triaity always play here. Belle Tue is the familiar headquarters of the Trinity team, and the match was also played at Belle Tue. All this seems vastly contradictory, but like many other problems it is easily explaine I. Santal Magna is the name—or perhaps it would be mere in keeping to say She designation—of the parish in which the Belle Vue ground is situated. This interesting fact I learnt from a public notice to which was attached a common or garden brick wall.

Waksfielders and Santa! Magnites rolled up rapidly and by 3 p.m. there WAS a goodly concourse of some 11,000 bursting-with-excitement enthusiasts, plastered thickly round the field. The latter hardly did credit to the standing of such a club as Wakefield Trinity, being destitute of touch flags, and anything worth calling a grand stand. It had four goal posts.two crossbars, and a fanco however,so there wag no chance of Warrington claiming the match by virtue of red tape. Very smart indeed did the home team look in their dark blue jer- seys with a broad red band remind the chest, and stock- ings to match—as the Society papers say. So far I have not seen a brighter or more suitable football cog- tume,and it rather out in the shade Warrington's well worn primrose and blue. " Fine feathers don't make fine birds "and this proverb fitted tan case well from a Warrington point of view.

Smack Bate is a better hand at winning the toss than Stoddart and as usual, he had the choice of PQ- on Saturday. The advantage which the slight slope gave therefore fell to Warrington at the outset. A new ball was pretty soon lifted skywards, and after sundry aereal trips finally settled down well within the I home half. Alec tlfe, the full back with a big name and I equally big kick, was soon tested and found wanting The Warrington forwards allowed of no liberties being taken and after they had nearly swept the field by a mighty rush they led up to a try which was placed to the credit of Hal- lam. Such an early score was an unexpected slice of luck for Warrington, and visions of ultimate triumph were soon fbating in the minds' eye of Lancashire spec- tators. A few of these were summarily " busted " by the result of fleesorn's goal kick. Still three points seemed a huge lot to be going on with. Nearly the whole of this half Wakefield had to defend as they little expected having to do. Warrington played with the dash which WAS characteristic of them earlier in the season, and the tackling on both sides was of a deadly cup-tie order. Then the luck changed with startling suddenness. The first time the Trinity entered Into the Warrington half Fairhurst unfortunately mulled a catch and Whittaker registered a try for Wakefield. Lock. wood's goal completed the discomfiture of the joyous Warringtonians. It was hard luck, for Warrington had pressed continuously for 25 out of the 35 minutes which elapsed before the interval, when Wakefield led by 5 points to 3.

The second half was a battle royal. Both sides knew the other's strength and struggled determinedly as a consequence. Even vet however, Warrington were the superior, both in smartness and forward strength. It was seldom that their line was seriously menaced,though a score would undoubtedly have corn* but for Isher• we'd's watchfulness in the centre. A couple of passing movements, the like of which have been strangers to Warrington of late, were brilliantly carried out, and Heesom had a glorious chance on the line when he parted to Hallam. One's sighs had hardly depar- ted before Moores threw away a certain try by misfiading, a cross-kick from is captain. After this Warrington deserved to lose. With victory in their grasp, the prize was let slip, and Wakefield eati;red the second round with the score unaltered. I don't think there is any boast in saying that the best team lost, but that dosn't bring the cup any nearer.

--- Isherwood was the best back on the field, his safe catches and tricky runs being splendid. Bate and Duck- worth far outshone their vis-a-vis, while Hallam and MooresElgolli was ha so wo ffeda tmod bbautttefroar dhvisa ns ut argeetatchkalni nwg aws oeuxrdechtaevde. been a failure. The Wakefield flyer Price proved less than an ornament. During the game I don't believe that he carried the ball 20 yards on the run, while there was little seen of him in defensive work. Lockwood was sute but slow,while all the other home backs were about on a par. The two full backs, B,scow and Metcalfe,were neither at their best,and made repeated mistakes. Bs. cow's great blunder was in standing so far back.He had frequently to run up to meet the ball,and get tackled in consequence. In the scrimmages the opposing eights were wellmimaotsctheads,pbruotmthineernetw. as no question as to War- rington's gunerior forward play in tne leoae. Barratt worked like a Trojan, Naylor, Deakin,Moreson,and Tay- lor being a

It was not much ‘,if a surprise to find Swinton again de P .tad. Toes' showed such signs of over-training at Oldham,that it was anticipated the Bradford team would be tog much for them on the Park Avenue ground. The score at the final read 7 points to 2in favour of Brad- ford. Oldham won pretty comfortably on their awn gro ,nd against Leeds, but gave rather a poor exhibi- tion. Thn gro IX triumph in first division encounters was gai rind by the dashing Widnesians, who simply pulver- ised Liyersedge. The latter club's glory had clearly de. parted, and after their four goals six tries licking will probably want to bury their heads in sand or something equally impenetrable. There will not be a better game in the Le time to-day than that at Widnes,when Hamlet, the Yorkshire champions—or nearly so—visit the chemieal town. Widnes are M favaurites for the en- counter. Runcorn, Rochdale Hornets, Salford, and Leigh, all enter the sec)nd round, while St. Helens, TO- dAsley, Wigan, Stockport, and Morecambe join War- ringtt n in mourning.

--- Warrington's desr friends, Hull Kingston Rovers, had an enjoyable outing against Hull Marlborough. With only half their team on they waltzed round the juniors to the tune of 46 points to nil. Ths most promising corn- batatants for the semi-finals at present seern to be Wid- nes or the licwoors as they meet in the fourth round, Bradford, Salford,and Batley. Widnes are the hope of Laocashire this season,and that they are making a strong (-ffort to wreA the cup from Yorkshire there is no doubt whatever.

St. Mary'a seen] to have been the victims of very bard luck in their cup-tie game with the wooden spoonista of the aecond diviaion, Fleetword. div.head: EARLESTOWN CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: EARLESTOWN CRICKET CLUB.

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of this club which was fairly attonded and held in the anteroom at the Viaduct Insti- tute. took place on Monday night, Mr.T.Orma.nd presid- ing. Tiler° were also preser.t Messrs. C. W. Emmett, J. Seddon, Liver3ag,e, and J. Owen (secretary), &3. The Chairman said it gave him pleasure to preside as there was seldom any matter of a debatable nature brought up,a circumstance which went to show that the committee was a most excellent one and was well cap- tained by the secrotary and assistant secretary and the captains of the different teams.

The Secretary then read the report and balance sheet which contained the following :—"The past year was in many respects an interesting one and though we did not win as ma 'y matches as we should like to have done, it is only fair ta say here that the players showed no fall- ing off whatever in the keenness and enthusiasm with which they conducted their matches. The first eleven took the field on 18 occasions, when six games were won, 6 lost, leaving 4 drawn, against 10 matches won and 5 los-. in the previous ye tr. The number of runs scored was 1964 for 152 wickets, averaging 12 140 runs per wicket,our opponents compiling 2,176 runs for 148 wickets, giving an average of 14.104. In the year 1896 our per centage is batting was 13.9 whilst the wickets we obtained cost 101 each. This comparison enables us te note that with the bat we are practically holding our own but on the other hand each wicket captured cost us exactly four runs more than in the previous year. The Institute Committee have again generously placed four bate and £2 in cash at our disposal, the bate have been awarded to Messrs. T. Marsh, Bell,Wainwright and Harrison, the £2 being equally divided betweed Messrs. Alderson and Clare, Hatton and J. Marsh, an additional las from the club funds going to T. Mitchell as a slight recognition of his services behind the wickets, a posi- tion in which he hardly ever fails to do himself justice. the match list is again a good one, most of the old clubs being retained with the addition of home and home matches with Royton, and one fixture with kagehester. The club membership stands at the present time at 111, over 30 If these were played more or less in matches last year. For the first time in our existence the Treasurer has to lament a balance on the wrong side of the accounts, the receipts, including a balance of £1 Is 9d., amount to £52 33. 4d., and the expenditure £53 93. 2d. leaving £1 59. 10d., due to the Treasurer. The Chairman thought the members would admit the report was a satisfactory sue when they looked at it from every standpoint.—Oa the proposition of Mr. C. W. Emmett, seconded by Mr.. T. Mitchell, the report and balance sheet were unanimously passed. _ THE ELECTION OF OFFICERS. .

The Chairman said it had been his pleasurable duty for some years to move the re-election of Mr. J. W. Emmett, as president of the club, and he was again pleased I to do so.-11r. Liversage seconded, and the proposition was carried.—Messrs. D. Harrison and F. Har wood were again appointed vice presidents, and Mr. T. Ormand was unanimously selected to again undertake the duties of treasurer.—The Chairman proposea the re-appointment of Mr. John Owen as secretary, and remarked that at the same time he wished to convey to him a hearty vote of thanks for the indefatigable manner in which he had looked after the interests of the club during the past 15 seasons.—Mr. W. Iluddleston seconded, and the re-ap- pointment met with the hearty approval of the members. Mr. J. H. Alderson was appointed assistant secretary.— Mr. C. W. Emmett was re-elected as captain of the first eleven. The appointment of vice-captain of the first team re- sulted, after voting by ballot, in the appointment of G., Huqband, the unsuccessful candidate being T. Mitchell. Similar contests occurred regarding the position of captain and vice-captain of tbe second eleven Mr. sanders ultimately being chosen in preference to W. Hattori for the firvt team captaincy and James Huddle.- ton being selected as vice-captain, F. Butler and W. Hatton being the other two candidates. The appointment of committee resulted as follows a proposition by Mr. C. W. Emmett that the whole com- mittee be re-elected en bloc having been defested:Meoqrs. Liversage, Roberts, T. Mitchell, J . Seddon.J . Ogden, W. Huddleston. G. Husband, Jenkinson.and J. Huddleaton. Ma personnel of committee was thus changed by the substitution of the names of Messrs. lenkinson and James Huddleston tor Ellose of Messrs. E. Scott and
Messrs. John Gooding and F.J.Ensmett were re-elected auditors.
The prism were then presented by Mr. Ormand who commented enlogisticslly noon the batting performances of T. Marsh as season and the all round play of J. Marsh for both elevens.
A vote of thanks having hen heartily accordol to Mr. Ormand that gentleman suitably responded. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: POPULAR LECTURES AT EA.RLESTO WN.
div.p: POPULAR LECTURES AT EA.RLESTO WN.
THE WORK OF FROST AND ICE.

The third of the series of lectures promoted by the Newton-in-Mskerfield, Lecture Committee was given in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Thursday evening by Mr. E. J. Garwood, M.A., F.G.S.. of Cambridge. Dr. Street,of Haydock,prmided, and there was again a large audience. Dr. Street said it was his pleasing duty to introduce to them the lecturer, Mr. Garwood. whose lecture on frost and ics they had been anticipating and looking for- ward to with pleasure. It might interest them to know that Mr. Garwood came back from the Arctic regions with Naniren, and was an intimate friend of N snaen'a,and he saw Professor Andres start for the North Psler in his balloon, 80 that his knowledge of ice and snow must be an intimate one. (Applause.) The Lrcturer spoke of the fascination that the subject had always enlisted in scientific men. This was due no doubt partly to the beauty of the scenery into which the observer of ice action was led, and the healthy character of the work, but also perhaps because it was a subject which lent itself admirably to controversy, and if there was one thing scientific men delighted in more than any other it was controversy. A critic, of modern scientific !methods recently remarked What a scientist aims at is net so much the exact truth as a good working hype- thesis which would enable him to bring out his book befere the other man's." But though this was of course a libel there was no doubt that more books and papers had been written about ice than about any other minor branch of science. Speaking of the characteristic scenery of the Alps and comparing it with that of our own country, the lecturer pointed out that this differ- ence was essentially due to the difference in the charac- ter of the chief denuding agents at work in the two cases, our own country being moulded into the soft and undulating curves characteristic of a humid climate. The mountain passes of the Alps were toeing carved out along their lines of weakness into pinnacles and precipices by the isolated action of frog, the drainage above the snow line being carried off by means of avalanches and glaciers. This was illustrated by photographs of typical peaks and glaviers in the Alps specially taken by the lecturer. After alluding to the proofs of glaciers motirin and touching on the various theories which had been propounded to account for these motions, he spoke of the geological work which tey performed in transporting loose debris and to some extant crowding the valleys, but considered that too much stress had been laid on this portion of their work by former geologists, especially by Professor Ramsey. In discussing the posqible excavation of lake basins by moving ice he pointed out that ne anthentic evidence of such an origin for any important lake had yet been brought forward. and quoted Mr. Moor's recent work on the origin of English lakes as proving that the damrraing of the old, and in the majority of cases the new valleys by dwelt of glacial moraine would amply account for their exigence. The latter portion of the lecture was devoted to a description of the scenery of the Arctic rogiona,most of the views shown being of the interior of Spiozhergen where the lecturer has spent the last two summers, He pointed out the simi- larity of the mountain forms to those of the Alps above the snow line, and mentioned the enormous rapidity with which deuedation by frost was proceeding. He I illustrated various points which could be studied in these regions which threw considerable light on such vexed questions in European glaciation as the formation of karnoa and erkers. the influence of submerged mountain ranges on the distribution of the ground and ex-glacial moraine,the distribution over the sea bottom of boulders transported by fl)atinw ice, and the formation of strati- fied and contorted boulder clay under land ice. In dis- cussing the possibility of material being upraised by moving ice and deposited at a high level than it source origin he Tio'ed a case which had crime under his own observation when raised beach material containing Shells,drift wood and bones of wales had been elevated up to 500 feet above its original level. The lecture was peofusely illustrated by numerous photographs.thrown on the screen by the oxy-hydrogen light, the lantern being manipulated by Mr. J. H. Graham. , • A vote of thanks ti the lecturer was accorded on the motion of the Rev. H. Monk, who spoke of the very pleasant evening he and the audience ha cT spent in Ilse teninEr, to a most interesting lecturer. Dr. Watkins seconded. A ,airnillr compliment was paid the Chairman, and the Min". 1137, dispersed.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday,Mr. J. Knowles presiding. There were also present Mr. A. R. Norman, .1.P., Mr. S. Yarwood, the members of the Rural District Council with Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), and Mr. G. F. Ashton (deputy clerk.) VISITING COMMITTEE.

Tho Vigiting C-o-in-m-irre—Te-pOr-t-ed that Mr. Arthur Rigby, and Mr. J. Mclntyre had presented periodicals and toys for the use of inmates. The master having re- ported that he was without a male assistant, it was re- commended that he procure temporary assistance. The minutes were approved of on the motion of Mr. Nerman seconded by Mr. Yarwood.

DR. BOIVBR'S SALARY. The Local Government Board wrote approving of the proposal of the Guardians to increase the salary of Dr. Blwer, medical officer for the Budworth district from £BO to £lOO per annum.

THE APPRBETICESNIP OF PAUPER CHILEREN. A letter was read from the Local Government Board with reference to the regulations with respect to the apprenticeship of pauper children. Cases sometimes occurred in which it was desirable that compliance with some of the requirements of the regulations on this sub- ject should be dispensed with and that difficulty arose owing to the want of a proviiion to enable them tc dis- pense with any of these requirements. As regarded a few unions the board bad met the difficulty by issuing a special order which enabled them to assent to a de- parture from the regulations in particular cases. And it seemed to the beard desirable that this provision should be extended to all poor law unions. They had therefore issued a general order on the subject.

div.head: REPAYMENT 0-F LOANS.
div.p: THE REPAYMENT 0-F LOANS.

A circular letter was read from Mr. L. F. Johnson, clerk to the Stockport Union calling attention to toe re- fusal of the Local Government Board to sanction a longer period than 30 years for Building Loans. They (the Stoskport Guardians) considered the subject should not be allowed to rest where it was, and with the object of obtaining some concession from the Local Govern- ment Boad, they had requested Mr. Sidebotham to raise the question in the Rouse of Commons. The Guardians would therefore be glad if the Runcorn Board would communicate with the local members of Parliament pointing out to them the great importartne r,f the ques- tion.—On the motion of Mr. Williams se,tonde.l by Mr. Wright it was decided to ask Sir J. T. Brunner, M.P., The Hon. Egerten Tattoo, M.P., apd Mr. Tollemaohe, M.P., to support Mr. Sidebotham. .

Choy decided to allow any boys who were &Amu: of joining the army or navy service to do 50.7-This was approved of.

pITTs' S, LONDON-ROAD, MANCHESTER. THE RENOWNED GENERAL FURNISHERS. LATEST PRESS OPINION. "Western Telegraph," of January 1, IE9B "Few houses in Manchester occupies( in the same line of business are better known or enjoy a larger share of patronage than that of Samuel Pitts, late of Gnythorn, now ofiLondon-road, Manchester, the complete house shop, and office furnisher. It was in 1845 that the present proprietor initiated the business, operations having been first com- menced by him in Brook-street as a cabinet maker and dealer In office furniture. By his energy and ability the concern prospered, and more accommodation becoming necessary, a move was made to the late premises in Gaythern about 26 years since. Samuel Pitts soon acquired a name for the superior excellence of the goods he supplied, the vast range of selection offered to customers, and the house advanced with rapid strides into a foremost and leading position in the trade. Just recently the Corporation purchased the Gay- thorn premises for streetimprovement purposes. and Samuel Pitts had once again to find • fresh gelds and pastures new.' This time his choice tell upon the vast edifice until latterly known as Borough Buildings, situate 100 to 120, London-road, which he has now converted into what is often termed the largest and most convenient general furnishing establishment in Man- chester. The premises occupied are enormous in extent and attractive in appearance, and are prominently and com- mandingly located. They comprise a magnificent frontagB of plate-glass windows, well stocked with high-class goods, together with extensive showrooms nearly 300 feet long on ' the ground floor, and offices and counting house. The first, second, and third floors are occupied by a number of stock and showrooms, and extended workshop accommodation is offered by the premises on the opposite side of London-road. The establishment throughout has been admirably arranged, and thoroughly and elegantly fitted up with every require- ment, including electsic light throughout, hydraulic pas- senger and luggage lift to all floors, for the effective display ef the splendid selection of goods, which cannot be surpassed by those of any competitor, either in extent, variety, or general superiority, in soundness of material, good work- manship, and elegance and novelty of &sign the house has no successful rivals in Manchester. while prices will always be found of the most satisfactory character. The proprietor is thoroughly acquainted with every eligible source of supply and in addition to his own special make the establishment displays the choicest specimen., both new and second-hand, of other well-known manufacturers. Samuel Pitts is a thoroughly practical man, and his personal supervision is bestowed upon the business in its entirety, He is able, ener- getio,and courteous in his control, and all his dealings are marked by his methods of strict fairness and honesty. In conclusion. we should strongly advise all furnishing, whether in part or throughout, to pay this establishment a visit. The same civility and courtesy is extended to all, whether buying or not, and the firm's well-known straightforward, syste- matic meth4 ensures all orders being satisfactorily exe- cuted. WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. A —O-EthTabove Council was held inßnew°s7eciyiliCahraYr;e,ling Wednesday afternoon, Mr. Wil- Ham Boughton p There Were also present : Messrs. T. Haltan, ,owe, J. Warburton, J. John- son, J. W. Knowil , T. Mather, J. Digreare, S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. S (medical officer), F. rfoot (nuisance inspector), - S. Stone (for Mr. W. Owen, surveyor), The CLERK announef. the total rail for general expenses for the next l r was £450 THE WATER DIFFICULTY AT PEDKETII. Mr. DIGNUM announced that water had been put in the 8 houses at Penketh from which there was a com- plaint as to the quality of the well water. ?IMPOSED LIGRI INC} OF WINWICK-ROAD. Mr.Kenawans said th t a leading ratepayer of Winwick had told him that he thought it was necessarv,now that the asylum was being built,and the amount of traffic in- creased, that the main road from Longford Bridge to Winwick Church should be lighted, Mr. Knowles said that the road had become rough and he thought they would not like a lady member of their families to tra- verse the road at night i's its present condition. He thought it was time the road was lighted. The CHAIRMAN reminded the Council that they would have no increase in rateahle value from the asylum until the building was complete 3. Mr. MATHER : We have been wanting lamps for a long time. Mr. DIGNUM : If there is a danger to the public I don't think there should be any delay in placing lamps. How long do you expr ce this buildine will be P Mr. KNOWLES: Seven or eight years. Mr. DioNum : Then it is a mistake to put the matter off. Mr. MATHER : I think there ought to be lamps before another winter. Mr. KNOWLES : We want proceedings now so that we can have them for winter. I move that the Clerk ask the Warrington Corporation their terms for lighting the road from the Borough Boundary to Winwick Church. Mr. DIGNUM seconded and it was agreed to unani- mously. WATER AT THE "CHAPEL HOUSE" The CLERK said he was in receipt of a letter dated February 19th, from Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Co.. stating that the water question at the " Chapel House" Inn, Burtonwood. would receive their attention next week. Ha had asked them to clean out the well. SUGGESTED NEW COUNCILLOR AND GUARDIAN FOR BI7RTONWOOD. A letter was read from he Clerk of the Burtonwood Parish Council stating that they thought the parish was insufficiently represented on the Warrington Board of Guardians and District Council and should have at least two members. Mr. WARBURTON : I think we should have two mem- bers. Mr. Manua: What is the population of Button- wood ? . Mr. Warburton : Between 15,000 and 16,000. The CHAIRMAN: What rateable value P The CLERK: It is a large one I know for a country township. Last September it v; as £15,376. It is the largest of the rural townships and most thickly popu- lated. The Chairmen : lam in entire sympathy with the ratepayers of Burtonwood. Mr. Dignum : Whose cansent is required ? The CLERK : The County Council's. The CHAIRMAN : It is the largest out-township in ex- tent. I don't think it is fairly represented by one Coun- cillor. Mr. KNOWLES moved that the Clerk take the necessary steps far Burtonwood to have another representative on the Guardians and District Council. Mr. WARistarroN seconded, and it was carried unani- mously. MR. I. W. KNOWLES, CC. The CLERK gave notice that John Wright Knowles bad been elected a county councillor for the Winwick divi- sion of the county of Lancaster. The CHAIRMAN : I must congratulate the new coun- cillor on the new appointment he has got. It is a very high honour well earned. Mr. KNOWLES replied. He would do all he could to further the interests of the District Council. He cer- tainly thought them was one department that ought to be attended to, and that was the roads of the district. (Hear, hear.) The reports of the Medical Officer, Inspector, and Sur- veyor, were read and passed, and the Council rose.
